c04.title: Intervals
c04.text:
Intervals are the vocabulary from which scales, chords and voice leading are built. This chapter gives them names and sizes, shows inversion, orders them by consonance and anchors each to a sound one knows. Chapter 1 treated the physical side; here the musical one.

## 4.1 Counting and names

An interval is the distance between two tones. Its name counts the natural tones from the lower to the upper tone including both: E–F is a second, E–G a third, E–A a fourth, E–B a fifth, E–C a sixth, E–D a seventh, E–E an octave. The same tone with itself is the unison. The counting ignores accidentals: E–G and E–G♯ are both thirds, but of different sizes.

[[c04-names]]

The example plays the eight intervals from E as melodic steps in E minor: E–E, E–F♯, E–G, E–A, E–B, E–C, E–D, E–E. One counts the letters: for E–B they are E F G A B, five, hence a fifth. Heard melodically an interval is a step or a leap; seconds are steps, everything larger is a leap.

## 4.2 Sizes

The size of an interval is measured in semitones. Seconds, thirds, sixths and sevenths occur in two basic sizes, minor and major; unison, fourth, fifth and octave in one, perfect. Minor second 1 semitone, major second 2, minor third 3, major third 4, perfect fourth 5, perfect fifth 7, minor sixth 8, major sixth 9, minor seventh 10, major seventh 11, octave 12. Between fourth and fifth lies the tritone with 6 semitones.

[[c04-twelve]]

The example lays out the twelve intervals over E4 in rising size, each as a dyad. Heard in succession, the sound opens increasingly from the second to the octave; the small intervals rub, the large ones carry.

[[c04-sizes]]

Minor and major lie a semitone apart: E–G is the minor third, E–G♯ the major; E–C the minor sixth, E–C♯ the major; E–F the minor second, E–F♯ the major; E–D the minor seventh, E–D♯ the major. The semitone decides between minor and major (chapter 5), between suspension and resolution (chapter 12) and how much gain an interval tolerates (chapter 1).

In general: a major or perfect interval enlarged by a semitone is augmented, a minor or perfect one reduced by a semitone is diminished.

[[c04-augdim]]

B–F is a diminished fifth (five letters, 6 semitones) and B–E♯ an augmented fourth on the same keys; the example writes F both times because in E minor F is the tone. C–D♯ is an augmented second (3 semitones), C–E♭ a minor third of the same size; the spelling distinguishes them, and chapter 5 shows where the augmented second occurs. D♯–C is a diminished seventh (9 semitones), as large as the major sixth D♯–C♯ would be; it is the interval of the diminished seventh chord (chapter 13). Finally the perfect fifth E–B as reference.

## 4.3 Inversion

If the lower tone is moved up an octave, the inversion of the interval results. The numbers add up to nine: a second becomes a seventh, a third a sixth, a fourth a fifth. The sizes swap: minor becomes major, augmented becomes diminished, perfect stays perfect. The semitones add up to twelve: minor third (3) and major sixth (9), perfect fourth (5) and perfect fifth (7).

[[c04-inversion]]

Each bar shows an interval and its inversion: E–G becomes G–E, minor third becomes major sixth; E–A becomes A–E, fourth becomes fifth; E–B becomes B–E, fifth becomes fourth; E–F♯ becomes F♯–E, major second becomes minor seventh. This complementarity is why the guitar strings are tuned in fourths and the bass in fourths although harmony thinks in fifths: a fourth upward reaches the same letter as a fifth downward (chapter 7).

## 4.4 Compound intervals

Intervals beyond the octave are called compound: ninth (second plus octave), tenth (third plus octave), eleventh (fourth plus octave), twelfth (fifth plus octave). For harmony they count like their simple forms; for sound they do not: a tenth is more open than a third.

[[c04-compound]]

The example sets each simple form against its compound one: third and tenth, fifth and twelfth, fourth and eleventh, finally the double octave E3–E4–E5. The tenth E3–G4 is the interval in which two guitars can play thirds without the difference tones of chapter 1 interfering: the third is there, but wide.

## 4.5 Consonance and dissonance

Unison, octave and fifth count as perfect consonances, thirds and sixths as imperfect. Seconds, sevenths and the tritone are dissonances. In two-part writing the fourth is a dissonance against the bass and a consonance between upper voices; chapter 18 explains why.

[[c04-consonance]]

Bar 1: fifth and octave, perfect; they sound empty and stable. Bar 2: the four thirds and sixths, imperfect; they sound full and have a colour, minor or major. Bars 3 and 4: seconds, seventh, tritone; they rub and demand a continuation. This classification describes the degree of fusion that chapter 1 derived from frequency ratios, and it determines how an interval is treated in part writing: dissonances are prepared and resolved, consonances may stand freely.

Under distortion the boundary shifts. The combination tones of chapter 1 turn the minor third in the low register into a practical dissonance and the fifth into the only interval that carries in every position. The rules of clean part writing remain valid; the rules of distorted part writing are added.

## 4.6 Intervals on the fingerboard and the keyboard

In pure-fourths tuning every interval has a single shape valid on all pairs of strings. The next higher string at the same fret is the fourth (5 semitones). Two frets higher on the next string is the fifth (5 + 2 = 7). Two frets lower the minor third (5 − 2 = 3), one fret lower the major third (5 − 1 = 4). Two strings higher and two frets higher is the octave (5 + 5 + 2 = 12).

[[c04-shapes]]

The example plays the fifth on all five string pairs with the lower string open: E2–B2, A2–E3, D3–A3, G3–D4, C4–G4. On the P4 guitar this is one and the same shape, second fret of the upper string. In standard tuning the shape changes at the transition to the B string because a semitone is missing there: the fifth above G3 would lie at the third fret. This geometry is the reason for P4 tuning.

On the keyboard one counts keys, black ones included: E–F is one key, E–F♯ two, E–G three. The white keys alone form the natural tones; where two white keys follow each other without a black one (E–F, B–C) lies the semitone.

## 4.7 Hearing intervals

Every interval can be anchored to a familiar sound, best of all to material from one's own repertoire.

[[c04-anchors]]

The minor third is the beginning of Em, E–G. The perfect fifth is the power chord. The minor second is the Phrygian step F–E, the semitone from above onto the root. The major sixth E–C♯ is the Dorian colour (chapter 6). The tritone B–F is the tension in the dominant seventh chord B7, which resolves to E–G or E–E (chapter 11). Intervals are heard reliably when both tones can be sung, the lower as reference and the upper as target.

## 4.8 Summary

- The name counts natural tones, the size counts semitones; both belong together.
- Second, third, sixth, seventh are minor or major; unison, fourth, fifth, octave are perfect.
- Augmented is a semitone larger than major or perfect, diminished a semitone smaller than minor or perfect.
- Inversion: numbers add to nine, semitones to twelve, minor becomes major, perfect stays perfect.
- Compound intervals count harmonically like simple ones but sound more open.
- Perfect: unison, fifth, octave. Imperfect: thirds, sixths. Dissonant: seconds, sevenths, tritone.
- In P4 tuning every interval has one shape; the fifth lies two frets higher on the next string.
- Every interval needs an anchor in the repertoire.

c05.title: Major, minor and the keys
c05.text:
Scales order the tone stock of a piece, keys give it a centre. This chapter introduces major and the three forms of minor, explains key signatures and the circle of fifths and shows how keys are related. At the end stands the question of what makes a key audible when no cadence confirms it; for the repertoire of this book it is the most important one.

## 5.1 The major scale

A scale is a sequence of tones within an octave, ordered by pitch. The major scale has seven degrees with the intervals whole tone, whole tone, semitone, whole tone, whole tone, whole tone, semitone (2-2-1-2-2-2-1). On C this gives the white keys C D E F G A B C. The semitones lie between the third and fourth and between the seventh and eighth degrees. The seventh degree is called the leading tone because it lies a semitone below the tonic and leads to it.

[[c05-major]]

The example plays the major scale on C and then on E. The pattern of intervals is the same; on E it needs four sharps (F♯ C♯ G♯ D♯) so that the semitones fall in the same places, between G♯ and A and between D♯ and E. On the P4 guitar this is one and the same fingering shifted by four frets; on the keyboard the picture of the black keys changes.

The degrees have names: tonic (1), supertonic (2), mediant (3), subdominant (4), dominant (5), submediant (6), leading tone (7). Tonic, subdominant and dominant are the primary degrees; the harmony of chapter 11 rests on them.

[[c05-degrees]]

The three primary degrees lie a fifth apart: the subdominant a fifth below the tonic, the dominant a fifth above. The example plays them as bass in E minor with the root in the upper voice: E, A, B, E. The same three tones are the three low open strings and the tones of the bass; chapter 7 draws the conclusions.

## 5.2 The minor scales

Natural minor has the intervals 2-1-2-2-1-2-2; on A it gives the white keys A B C D E F G A, on E the tones E F♯ G A B C D E. It contains no leading tone: the seventh degree lies a whole tone below the tonic. So that a dominant with a leading tone can arise, the seventh degree is raised by a semitone. That gives harmonic minor: E F♯ G A B C D♯ E. Between the sixth and seventh degrees an augmented second arises (C–D♯, three semitones), which sounds awkward in a melody.

Melodic minor raises the sixth degree as well and smooths the path to the leading tone: E F♯ G A B C♯ D♯ E ascending. Descending, where no leading tone is needed, one traditionally returns to natural minor.

[[c05-minor3]]

The example shows the three forms in turn over an E pedal, then an application: over Am the melody rises with C♯ and D♯ to the dominant B7; after the return to Em it falls with D and C.

[[c05-augsec]]

The difference in detail: bar 1 goes B–C–D♯–E, with the augmented second C–D♯, which sounds oriental or Baroque-pathetic and occurs in this music as a colour, but rarely as everyday material. Bar 2 goes B–C♯–D♯–E, smoothed, the melodic minor. Bar 3 falls E–D–C–B in natural minor: no leading tone is needed because the line leads away from the root, not toward it. In the practice of the references: chords follow harmonic minor (the dominant is major), melodies follow melodic minor ascending and natural minor descending, and everything that does not prepare a cadence stays in natural minor. Chapter 6 shows that natural minor is at the same time a mode, the Aeolian.

## 5.3 Key signatures and the circle of fifths

Every major scale except C major needs accidentals. Starting a fifth higher adds a sharp: G major has F♯, D major F♯ and C♯, A major F♯ C♯ G♯, E major four sharps. Starting a fifth lower adds a flat: F major has B♭, B♭ major B♭ and E♭. The sharps appear in the order F C G D A E B, the flats in the order B E A D G C F.

[[c05-circle]]

The example walks the circle as a tone sequence: C, G, D, A, E, B in fifths upward, each step one sharp more; then from C, F, B♭, E♭, A♭ in fourths upward, each step one flat more. Arranging the keys in a circle this way gives the circle of fifths; after twelve steps it closes, F♯ major and G♭ major coinciding enharmonically. Two rules for reading: the last sharp of the signature lies a semitone below the major tonic. The second-to-last flat is the major tonic.

## 5.4 Relative and parallel keys

Every major key has a minor key with the same signature, its relative minor: it begins a minor third lower. G major and E minor share the F♯, C major and A minor have no accidentals, F major and D minor share the B♭.

[[c05-relative]]

Both scales of the example carry one sharp; they consist of the same seven tones and differ only in which tone counts as the centre. A piece in E minor that lingers on G sounds for moments like G major without changing the signature; that is the most common brightening effect in minor and the basis of the mediant harmony in chapter 11.

The parallel key has the same tonic with the other mode: E major and E minor. Three accidentals lie between them because third, sixth and seventh change.

[[c05-parallel]]

The example sets the E major triad, broken and as a chord, beside the E minor triad. One tone, G♯ or G, decides the mode. Chapter 8 treats the triad; here the observation suffices that major and minor on the same root are closer to each other than they are on paper: the Picardy third (chapter 11) uses exactly this closeness.

The three centres of this book, E, A and D, sit next to each other in the circle of fifths: E minor (one sharp), A minor (none), D minor (one flat). Their parallel majors E, A and D have four, three and two sharps. Changes between neighbouring keys are soft because they share almost all tones; changes across several steps are hard. Chapter 13 treats these routes as modulation.

## 5.5 The key as sound

A key is more than its signature. It becomes audible when one tone appears as the centre: through duration, recurrence, low register and closing position. A piece in E minor can linger long on C or D without leaving the key as long as E remains the reference to which everything returns.

[[c05-pedal]]

The example holds E in the bass while the melody wanders through the whole stock of E minor. No chord changes, no cadence confirms the key, and still E minor is unambiguous at every moment: the pedal is the simplest form of a key. The references often confirm the key exactly so, through the sustained or recurring root, not through cadences; chapter 11 draws the line between modal and tonal confirmation.

## 5.6 Summary

- Major: 2-2-1-2-2-2-1, semitones between 3–4 and 7–8; the 7 is the leading tone.
- Natural minor: 2-1-2-2-1-2-2, no leading tone. Harmonic: 7 raised. Melodic: 6 and 7 raised, natural descending.
- Chords follow harmonic minor, melodies melodic minor ascending and natural minor descending.
- Fifths upward give sharps in the order F C G D A E B, fourths upward flats in the order B E A D G C F.
- Relative keys share the signature (G major, E minor); parallel keys share the tonic (E major, E minor).
- E, A, D are neighbours in the circle of fifths; changes between them are soft.
- A key becomes audible through its centre; the pedal is its simplest form.

c06.title: Modes, pentatonic, chromaticism
c06.text:
The modes are older than major and minor and more alive in this music: what distinguishes slow metal from pop is often that it thinks modally, not functionally. This chapter introduces the seven modes, shows that the bass decides the mode, and treats the pentatonic and chromatic scales as the two stocks that are smaller and larger than the scale.

## 6.1 The seven modes

The white keys contain seven scales, depending on which tone counts as the root: C Ionian (the major scale), D Dorian, E Phrygian, F Lydian, G Mixolydian, A Aeolian (natural minor), B Locrian. All seven consist of the same tones; they differ in the position of the two semitones relative to the root. The names come from the Middle Ages; the scales are older than major and minor.

The intervals: Ionian 2-2-1-2-2-2-1, Dorian 2-1-2-2-2-1-2, Phrygian 1-2-2-2-1-2-2, Lydian 2-2-2-1-2-2-1, Mixolydian 2-2-1-2-2-1-2, Aeolian 2-1-2-2-1-2-2, Locrian 1-2-2-1-2-2-2. Every mode can be transposed to any root. Over E: E Ionian is E major with four sharps, E Aeolian is E minor with one, E Phrygian has no accidentals, E Lydian has five sharps.

## 6.2 Characteristic tones and brightness

Ordering the modes by the number of sharps at the same root gives a series from bright to dark: Lydian, Ionian, Mixolydian, Dorian, Aeolian, Phrygian, Locrian. Each step lowers exactly one tone: the raised fourth becomes perfect (Lydian → Ionian), the major seventh minor (→ Mixolydian), the major third minor (→ Dorian), the major sixth minor (→ Aeolian), the major second minor (→ Phrygian), the perfect fifth diminished (→ Locrian). The tone changed last is also the characteristic tone of the mode: the ♯4 in Lydian, the ♭7 in Mixolydian, the 6 in Dorian, the ♭6 in Aeolian, the ♭2 in Phrygian.

[[c06-modes7]]

The example plays the seven modes over E in this order; from bar to bar a single tone changes. Locrian has no perfect fifth and does not work as the centre of a piece; it appears only in passing.

## 6.3 Modality: the bass decides

Since all modes can contain the same tones, it is not the pitch set that decides the mode but the centre.

[[c06-bass]]

The melody of the example stays the same in all eight bars, G F♯ E D E F♯, nothing but tones from E minor. Heard over E it is Aeolian; over C the same stock becomes C Lydian, because F♯ is now the raised fourth of C; over D, D Mixolydian, because C is the minor seventh of D; over A, A Dorian, because F♯ is the major sixth of A. A piece can change its mode without introducing a single new tone: it is enough for the bass to take a different centre.

[[c06-colours]]

Conversely, over a fixed bass a single tone changes the colour. The example holds E in the bass and changes one melody tone from bar to bar: F makes Phrygian, F♯ Aeolian, C♯ Dorian, G♯ major. The contour stays, the colour moves from dark to bright.

For the repertoire of this book four modes are central. Aeolian is the base colour; its characteristic tone ♭6 (C in E) and the step ♭6–5 are the most common closing move. Phrygian darkens through ♭2; the step F–E is a semitone close into the root, more final than C–B. Dorian brightens minor through the major sixth without becoming major. In this music Lydian usually arises not from new tones but from a bass on C or F beneath the E minor set.

[[c06-closes]]

The four closing moves over an E pedal: F–E is the Phrygian semitone from above; C–B the Aeolian semitone onto the fifth; D–E the whole-tone step from below, the modal close without leading tone; D♯–E the leading tone, the tonal close. Each of these four moves is enough to end a riff, and each has a different degree of finality: the leading tone is the most closed, the whole tone the most open.

[[c06-dorian]]

Dorian in the chord: the fourth degree of E minor is Am (A C E) in Aeolian, A (A C♯ E) in Dorian. One tone of the inner voice changes, and the move Em–A sounds brighter and more floating than Em–Am without leaving the base colour of minor.

## 6.4 The pentatonic scale

The minor pentatonic has five tones: root, minor third, fourth, fifth, minor seventh, in E thus E G A B D. It is the Aeolian without the second and sixth degrees, i.e. without the two tones that create semitone steps. That is why any sequence of its tones sounds consonant over an E bass, and why it is the usual material for solos over power chords.

[[c06-pentatonic]]

The example plays the minor pentatonic on E and then the major pentatonic on G: the same five tones, begun from the third tone and heard over a G bass. The major pentatonic on E itself would be E F♯ G♯ B C♯. What separates minor and major pentatonic is, as with the modes, only the centre.

[[c06-melody]]

The example leads a pentatonic melody over a bass that alternates between E and other roots. Five tones demand all the more shaping through rhythm, repetition, rest and target tone, because the pitches alone carry little tension; chapter 19 treats melody as a whole.

## 6.5 Chromaticism

Chromatic tones do not belong to the scale. They occur as passing tones between two scale tones, as neighbour tones circling a target, and as members of chords foreign to the key (chapter 13). A chromatic tone is named and spelled after its target: it gets a sharp when it continues upward and a flat when it continues downward.

[[c06-chromatic]]

Bar 1: E♭ as a passing tone between E and D, written with a flat because it goes downward. Bar 2: D♯ and F as lower and upper neighbours of E, the sharp shows the way upward. Bars 3 and 4: the chromatic scale from E4 to E5, ascending with sharps. It has twelve semitones and is not a mode but the stock from which all modes draw.

## 6.6 Summary

- Seven modes from the same tones; they differ in the position of the semitones relative to the root.
- Brightness: Lydian, Ionian, Mixolydian, Dorian, Aeolian, Phrygian, Locrian; every step lowers one tone.
- Characteristic tones: ♯4 Lydian, ♭7 Mixolydian, 6 Dorian, ♭6 Aeolian, ♭2 Phrygian.
- The bass decides the mode; the same melody over another bass is another mode.
- Four closing moves over E: F–E, C–B, D–E, D♯–E, from the most open to the most closed.
- Minor pentatonic: Aeolian without 2 and ♭6; over a root it is always consonant.
- Chromatic tones are named after their target: sharp upward, flat downward.

c07.title: Tuning and instrument
c07.text:
The tuning of an instrument is not a side issue of technique but a musical decision: it determines which tones sound open, which fingerings are easy and which intervals lie under the hand. This chapter explains why the low strings are called E A D, what pure-fourths tuning changes, what low tunings enforce and how Biber uses retuning as a compositional device.

## 7.1 The chain of fourths

The four low strings of the guitar and the four strings of the bass are tuned in perfect fourths: E A D G. Fourth and fifth complete each other to the octave, which is why a fourth upward reaches the same letter as a fifth downward.

[[c07-chain]]

Bars 1 and 2 show it: E up a fourth is A, E down a fifth is also A, an octave lower. Bar 3 plays the string chain E A D G in fourths upward, bar 4 the same tones backwards, G D A E, and that is a chain of fifths downward. The strings are therefore also a segment of the circle of fifths read backwards: going up the strings means going around the circle toward the subdominant.

For the harmony of this book the first three tones, E, A and D, are at the same time the three centres. Read in A, D is the subdominant and E the dominant: the cadence axis. Read in E, A is the subdominant and D the seventh degree without a leading tone: the modal axis. Read in D, A is the dominant and E the second degree.

[[c07-axes]]

The example plays the same basses twice. In A major, A, D, E, A give the cadence I–IV–V–I; the E carries a major chord with the leading tone G♯ and presses toward A. In E minor, E, A, D, E give the move i–iv–VII–i; the D carries a major chord without leading tone and returns to E by a whole-tone step. The same three open strings therefore carry a functional and a modal reading (chapter 11).

## 7.2 Standard tuning and pure fourths

Standard tuning E A D G B E breaks the chain of fourths between G and B with a major third. The reason is historical and practical: five fourths across six strings span two octaves and a semitone (E2 to F4), six strings with one third span exactly two octaves (E2 to E4), and the common major and minor shapes fall under four fingers. The price is an irregularity: every interval shape changes by one fret at the transition to the B string.

Pure-fourths tuning E A D G C F keeps the chain. Every interval has a single shape valid on all pairs of strings (chapter 4). Scales lie the same in every position, chord shapes can be moved freely, and the two high strings reach a semitone higher than in standard tuning.

[[c07-shape]]

The example plays one four-tone fingering, frets 0 3 0 2 across two strings, on four string pairs: E G A B on strings 6 and 5, A C D E on 5 and 4, G B♭ C D on 3 and 2, C E♭ F G on 2 and 1. Each time it is the same figure a fourth higher; the intervals within the figure stay the same. In standard tuning the same fingering on strings 3 and 2 would give G B♭ B C♯, because the B string lies a semitone lower: the figure would be a different one.

The price of fourths tuning: the familiar shapes of standard tuning do not apply, open chords in E and A sound different, and the literature for guitar in standard tuning has to be reread. This book writes notation with position marks and not tablature, so that the music stays readable regardless of tuning.

[[c07-harmonics]]

The six open strings of P4 tuning as harmonics over the twelfth fret: they sound an octave above the open string, E3 A3 D4 G4 C5 F5, and form the same chain of fourths.

## 7.3 Low tunings

Type O Negative tune the guitar on *October Rust* to B standard: B E A D F♯ B, all six strings a fourth lower than standard. The shapes stay, every tone sounds a fourth lower; an E shape sounds as B. The lowest string sits at B1 with 61.7 Hz.

[[c07-bstandard]]

The example writes the power-chord shape on the fifth string, which gives A5 in standard tuning (A2 E3 A3), and beside it what the same shape sounds in B standard: E5 (E2 B2 E3). The player fingers A and hears E. What the low tuning enforces follows from chapter 1: thirds move upward or vanish from the guitar, chords widen, the bass can no longer sit below the guitar and doubles it or goes lower still with effects, and the keyboards take over the register above C4. The heavy string gauge a low tuning needs at equal tension is calculated in appendix A.

## 7.4 Scordatura

Retuning as a compositional device is old. In the *Harmonia artificioso-ariosa* Biber writes six of the seven partitas for retuned instruments; only the sixth is in normal tuning. The tunings are part of the work and enable chords and resonances unreachable in normal tuning.

[[c07-scordatura]]

Bar 1 shows the open strings of the violin in normal tuning, G3 D4 A4 E5, a chain of fifths. Bar 2 the tuning of both violins in the first partita, A3 E4 A4 D5: fifth, fourth, fourth, with two A's that, as the root of D minor's dominant, reinforce it. Bars 3 and 4 the tuning of the two violas d'amore in the seventh partita, C3 G3 C4 E♭4 G4 C5, a broken C minor chord; beneath lie sympathetic strings that vibrate by themselves. Appendix A lists all the tunings. Scordatura notation shows fingerings, not sounding tones: the player reads as if the instrument were tuned normally, and the instrument produces the sounding pitch.

P4, B standard and Biber's tunings follow the same idea: the tuning chooses which sounds are easily reachable, and thereby the music. An instrument in fourths favours quartal sounds and movable shapes; one tuned to a chord favours that chord and its resonance.

## 7.5 The instruments of this book

[[c07-ranges]]

The P4 guitar sounds from E2 to F4 on open strings and up to about C6 in high positions; it can carry foundation (open bass strings), riff, inner voice and line, but a pad only clean and with reverb. The 49-key keyboard runs from C2 to C6 and carries foundation, pad and line; the left hand usually lies below C4, the right above. The violin, the instrument of Biber and Vivaldi and the third voice of My Dying Bride, is tuned in fifths, G3 D4 A4 E5, and sits in the soprano register. The bass runs from E1 upward, an octave below the low guitar string and below the range of this book's notated examples, up to about G4, and takes the foundation alone. Chapter 20 assigns the roles in the texture to these registers.

## 7.6 Summary

- A fourth up and a fifth down reach the same letter; the strings E A D G are a piece of the circle of fifths.
- E, A, D are the cadence axis in A (IV, V) and the modal axis in E (iv, VII).
- Standard tuning breaks the chain with a third; P4 keeps it and makes every shape movable.
- Low tuning lowers every fingering by the same distance; thirds move upward, keyboards take the register above.
- Scordatura chooses the tones that are easily reachable and writes fingerings instead of sounding tones.
- Guitar E2–F4 open, keyboard C2–C6, violin G3–E5 open, bass from E1.

c08.title: Triads
c08.text:
The triad is the basic unit of harmony: three tones heard together as one sound. This chapter builds it from thirds, shows its four types, its inversions and spacings, derives the diatonic triads from the scale and assigns them functions. It is the foundation of chapters 9 to 14.

## 8.1 Construction and types

A triad consists of three tones a third apart: root, third and fifth. Four types arise from the sizes of the two thirds. The major triad stacks a major third with a minor one above (4 + 3 semitones, E G♯ B); the minor triad a minor third with a major above (3 + 4, E G B); the diminished triad two minor thirds (3 + 3, E G B♭); the augmented two major (4 + 4, E G♯ B♯). Major and minor have a perfect fifth and are consonant; the diminished has a diminished, the augmented an augmented fifth, and both are dissonant and press onward.

[[c08-types]]

The example plays the four types over the same root E. One hears: major bright and stable, minor dark and stable, diminished tight and pressing, augmented floating and without ground, because its fifth B♯ is enharmonically C and the chord divides the octave into three equal parts.

The difference between major and minor lies solely in the third. Over an E bass, G♯ or G decides whether the sound is bright or dark; the fifth B is common to both.

[[c08-third]]

The bass holds the power chord E–B through all four bars. Without a third (bars 1 and 4) the sound is neither major nor minor; with G♯ above (bar 2) it is E major, with G (bar 3) E minor. A single tone in an upper voice decides the mode of the whole sound; that is why a power chord can be either and is neither (chapter 9).

## 8.2 Inversion and spacing

A triad remains the same chord whichever of its tones lies at the bottom. With the root in the bass it is in root position; with the third in the bass in first inversion (sixth chord); with the fifth in the bass in second inversion (six-four chord). The names come from the intervals above the bass: in first inversion third and sixth lie above the bass, in second inversion fourth and sixth.

[[c08-inversions]]

The three tones E, G and B stay the same; only the bass tone moves. Over E the sound is stable and heavy; over G light and mobile, the typical passing sound; over B dissonant against the bass, because the fourth E above B presses toward D♯, and therefore a sound that wants to resolve: the six-four chord stands before the dominant, not in its place. The figures in the labels are the thoroughbass figures that chapter 10 explains.

Spacing must be distinguished from inversion: the distribution of the tones above the bass. In close position the three tones lie within an octave, in open position with gaps. Em as E2, B3, G4 is the same inversion as E4, G4, B4 but sounds entirely different. Open position with a low root and a high third is the default of this music because the third then stays out of the range of the combination tones (chapter 1).

[[c08-spacing]]

The example contrasts Em close and open, then the two inversions with G and B in the bass, then the four types over the same E. Close position sounds compact and carries on the keyboard; open position sounds large and is the position of the guitar, whose strings in fourths enforce wide shapes anyway.

## 8.3 Diatonic triads

On every degree of a scale a triad arises from its tones. In major, degrees I, IV and V are major, II, III and VI minor, VII diminished. In natural minor (Aeolian), i, iv and v are minor, III, VI and VII major, ii diminished. The degrees are labelled with Roman numerals, upper case for major, lower case for minor, with ° for diminished and + for augmented.

[[c08-diatonic]]

E Aeolian: i Em, ii° F♯dim, III G, iv Am, v Bm, VI C, VII D. Three minor, three major, one diminished; the major chords lie on III, VI and VII, and those are the chords that give minor its bright side without leaving it. The example climbs the degrees as chords in close position.

Harmonic minor changes three chords: v becomes major (B), VII becomes diminished (D♯dim), III becomes augmented (G+).

[[c08-harmonic]]

The example precedes each changed chord with its Aeolian form: Bm and B, D and D♯dim, G and G+. In practice the first of these changes usually suffices: the major dominant B is the tonal chord in an otherwise modal surrounding. Melodic minor additionally makes ii minor (F♯m) and IV major (A), which corresponds to Dorian (chapter 6).

## 8.4 Functions

Functional theory gathers the degrees into three groups: tonic (I, with III and VI as substitutes), subdominant (IV, with II as substitute), dominant (V, with VII as substitute). The letters T, S and D denote them in major, t, s and d in minor; an appended P (German Parallele, here R for relative) denotes the relative, the substitute in the other mode.

[[c08-functions]]

A piece in E minor has the tonic Em, the subdominant Am, the dominant B (with leading tone) or Bm (without). Bars 1 to 4 show the cadence t–s–D–t; bars 5 to 8 replace the tonic by its relative C and the dominant by the relative D. C and D, the major chords on VI and VII, are the characteristic chords of the modal; functional theory reads them as tonic relative and dominant relative, modal hearing takes them as colours of their own over the centre E. Both readings are correct; which applies depends on whether a leading tone is in play (chapter 11).

## 8.5 Triads on guitar and keyboard

On the keyboard the close triad lies under one hand: 1–3–5 for the right hand in root position, the inversions by shifting one finger. Open spacing arises when the left hand takes the root low and the right hand third and fifth above. On the P4 guitar root, fifth and octave lie on three neighbouring strings in the same shape as the power chord, and the third is added on the next string: the major third one fret below the fourth shape, the minor third two frets below.

[[c08-hands]]

The example sets both voicings side by side: on the keyboard Em and Am close in the right hand over the low root of the left; on the guitar E2 B2 E3 G3 and A2 E3 A3 C4, power-chord shape with the minor third on the fourth string. Both are the same chord in open position. All guitar shapes transfer to every pair of strings and every position; open strings cannot be moved along.

## 8.6 Summary

- Triad: root, third, fifth; the sizes of the two thirds give major, minor, diminished, augmented.
- The third decides the mode; the fifth is common to major and minor.
- Inversion: the bass tone; spacing: the distribution above it. Open spacing with a high third is the default under gain.
- E Aeolian: i ii° III iv v VI VII; harmonic minor turns v into V.
- Functions: t, s, D; the relatives C and D are the colours of the modal.
- Keyboard: close in the right hand, root in the left. Guitar: power-chord shape plus third on the next string.

c09.title: Chords without thirds: power chord, fourths, suspended chords
c09.text:
Distorted music has its own chord theory: it begins not with the triad but with the power chord, the sound of root and fifth. This chapter explains why it works under gain, shows its shapes and registers, and treats the other chords without thirds, suspended chords and quartal stacks, which lie especially close on the P4 guitar.

## 9.1 The power chord

A power chord is a root with its fifth, often with the octave above: 1–5 or 1–5–8. It has no third and is therefore neither major nor minor. The symbol writes a 5 after the root: E5, A5, D5. Calling it a chord is generous, since two tones strictly form a dyad; musically, however, the power chord takes on in distorted music the role the triad has in clean writing, and the third is supplied by the context: the voice, the keyboard, the melody, or nobody.

Why the fifth in particular: chapter 1 showed that root and fifth under distortion produce combination tones that are themselves chord tones, namely the root an octave lower. The power chord reinforces itself. Every triad with a third, by contrast, produces foreign tones that get louder the lower the third lies.

## 9.2 Shapes and registers

On the P4 guitar the fifth lies one string higher and two frets further than the root, the octave two strings higher and two frets further. The third shape is the inverted fifth, i.e. the fourth: fifth below, root above, for example B2–E3. It lies on two neighbouring strings at the same fret and sounds heavier than the fifth shape because the root is on top and the difference tone, the root an octave below the upper tone, replaces the missing bass.

[[c09-power]]

The example shows the three shapes over E and then the power chords on the three open bass strings E, A and D: the chain of fourths from chapter 7 as a riff. All shapes transfer to every position.

[[c09-register]]

The same power chord in three registers: E2–B2 is the riff register, heavy and with the difference tone E1; E3–B3 is the middle register, in which a second guitarist can play above the riff; E4–B4 is high and light, a sound for lines and pads. Finally the fourth shape B2–E3: the same letters as the first, but turned, with the root on top.

## 9.3 The third from the context

[[c09-context]]

The example holds E5 with octave in the bass and places above it once G and once G♯ as a melody tone. The listener hears Em and E major although the guitar plays the same thing both times. That is the division of labour in the references: the distorted guitar carries root and fifth in the low register, thirds appear in the keyboards, the violin, the voice or in high guitar positions with less gain. Whoever plays alone must achieve this distribution on one instrument: power chord low, third high, or power chord and then the third as a melody tone.

[[c09-riff]]

A riff of power chords is a bass line with reinforcement. The example goes E5–A5–B5–E5, i.e. i–iv–v–i without thirds, with muted eighths between the chords; whether the music is major or minor is decided by the other voices. Chords without thirds are not a substitute for harmony but its relocation.

## 9.4 Suspended chords

A suspended chord replaces the third with its neighbour: sus4 with the fourth (Esus4 = E A B), sus2 with the second (Esus2 = E F♯ B). The name comes from the suspension (chapter 18): historically the fourth was a tone held over from the previous chord that then resolved into the third.

[[c09-sus]]

Bars 1 to 4 set Esus4 and Esus2 beside E major and E minor: the fifth stays, the middle tone moves A, F♯, G♯, G. Bars 5 and 6 show the historical form, sus4 as a suspension resolving into the third: A moves to G♯. In the modal music of the references the sus chord also stands on its own, as a sound without mode but with tension, and does not resolve. Both suspended chords are usable under distortion because their tones stand in pure intervals to the root: fourth, fifth, major second.

## 9.5 Quartal voicing

Stacking fourths instead of thirds yields sounds such as E–A–D or A–D–G. They contain no third and no fifth to the lowest tone but fourth and minor seventh, and are therefore open: they can be read differently over different basses.

[[c09-stacks]]

On the P4 guitar a quartal stack lies on three strings at the same fret; the open strings themselves are four such sounds: E–A–D, A–D–G, D–G–C, G–C–F. It is the simplest form of the tuning itself, and every fingering that takes three strings at the same fret produces it at another height.

[[c09-quartal]]

The example holds E–A–D on the middle strings and changes the bass; the sound stays the same, its meaning shifts. E–A–D over E is Esus4 with a seventh, over A an Asus2 sound with fifth, over D a Dsus2 with the fifth in the bass, over C a fragment of Cmaj9. This ambiguity makes quartal sounds ideal pads: they contradict no bass.

## 9.6 Summary

- Power chord: 1–5 or 1–5–8, without third, neither major nor minor; its difference tone is its own root.
- Three shapes: fifth, fifth with octave, fourth shape; all in every position.
- Low is the riff register, middle the register of the second guitar, high that of the line.
- The third comes from the context: voice, keyboard, melody or nobody.
- sus4 and sus2 replace the third with its neighbour; they withstand gain because their intervals are pure.
- Quartal stacks are open and fit many basses; on the P4 guitar they are one fingering at the same fret.

c10-types.title: The five seventh-chord types over E: dominant, major, minor, half-diminished, diminished

c10-diatonic.title: The diatonic seventh chords of E Aeolian

c10-resolve.title: The seventh falls: A to G in B7–Em; the major seventh B stays put in Cmaj7–Em7

c10-added.title: Additions over Em: add9 without seventh, 6, 9 with seventh, maj7 from harmonic minor

c10-symbols.title: Eight symbols, eight voicings: Em7, Emadd9, Esus4, Esus2, Cmaj7, Cmaj7/E, Em/C, B7♭9

c10.title: Seventh chords and chord symbols
c10.text:
With the seventh, harmony begins to have direction. This chapter builds the four-note chords, orders the symbol notation that names them, and shows two older scripts for the same thing: Roman numerals with inversion figures and the thoroughbass in which Vivaldi and Biber write their accompaniment. Whoever can read all three can read every score and every lead sheet.

## 10.1 Seventh chords

Stacking a further third on the triad gives a four-note chord, the seventh chord. The seventh is a dissonance against the root and gives the chord a direction: it wants to fall by step. Five types are common.

[[c10-types]]

The dominant seventh (major with minor seventh, E7 = E G♯ B D) is the chord of the dominant. The major seventh chord (major with major seventh, Emaj7 = E G♯ B D♯) is soft and usually stands on I and IV. The minor seventh chord (minor with minor seventh, Em7 = E G B D) is the default on ii, iii, vi in major and on i, iv, v in minor. The half-diminished seventh (diminished with minor seventh, Em7♭5 = E G B♭ D) stands on ii in minor. The diminished seventh (diminished with diminished seventh, Edim7 = E G B♭ D♭) stands on vii in harmonic minor; chapter 13 treats its ambiguity. The example builds all five over E so that the differences become audible one tone per step.

[[c10-diatonic]]

Diatonic seventh chords in E Aeolian: Em7, F♯m7♭5, Gmaj7, Am7, Bm7, Cmaj7, D7. In harmonic minor Bm7 becomes B7 and D7 becomes D♯dim7. The minor chord with major seventh (Em(maj7) = E G B D♯) arises from harmonic minor on the first degree and sounds tense.

[[c10-resolve]]

What the seventh does: in B7–Em, A, the seventh, falls to G, the third of the tonic, while D♯ rises to E and B stays. In Cmaj7–Em7 the major seventh B stays as a common tone; it is not a dissonance that pushes but a colour that rests. That is the difference between the dominant seventh, which has direction, and the major seventh chord, which needs none.

## 10.2 Sixth, add and ninth chords

A sixth chord in the sense of symbol notation adds the major sixth to the triad: E6 = E G♯ B C♯, Em6 = E G B C♯. An add chord adds a tone without the seventh: Eadd9 = E G♯ B F♯, Emadd9 = E G B F♯. If the chord contains the seventh, the extensions are called 9, 11 and 13: E9 = E G♯ B D F♯, Em9 = E G B D F♯, Emaj9 = E G♯ B D♯ F♯. With 11 the third is usually omitted because it rubs against the eleventh; with 13 the eleventh is omitted. Alterations stand in brackets or appended: B7♭9 = B D♯ F♯ A C, B7♯9, B7♭5, Cmaj7♯11.

[[c10-added]]

Four colours over E: Emadd9 with the ninth F♯ and without seventh, soft and without direction; Em6 with the Dorian C♯; Em9 with seventh and ninth, denser; Em(maj7) with D♯, tense. For the references two of them matter: madd9 as a pad without direction, as Anathema use it in clean guitars and keyboards, and maj7 on VI (Cmaj7 in E minor), which turns the Aeolian C into a resting sound. Dominant sevenths appear constantly in Vivaldi and Biber and rarely in the metal references, because they create direction.

## 10.3 The system of symbols

A chord symbol is read from left to right: root; quality (nothing for major, m for minor, dim or ° for diminished, aug or + for augmented); seventh (7 for the minor, maj7 or Δ for the major); extensions (9, 11, 13); alterations (♭5, ♯5, ♭9, ♯9, ♯11, ♭13); additions (add); omissions (no3, no5); bass tone after a slash. The symbol fixes the tones, not their spacing, doubling or duration. Two players with the same symbol play different voicings. Appendix D lists all symbols with their tones over E, A and D.

[[c10-symbols]]

The example shows eight symbols in one voicing each. Bars 5 and 7 have the same upper voices G B E over a C in the bass; the bass determines the name: Em/C is not an Em over C but a Cmaj7 without a doubled root.

[[c10-slash]]

The slash therefore denotes either an inversion or a chord that is really called something else. Em/G and Em/B are inversions because G and B are chord tones. Em/C is Cmaj7 because C is not a tone of Em and the bass supplies the root. D/E is an Esus sound with ninth, E D F♯ A, usually written E9sus4: the colour of the Anathema pads over a sustained E. Rule: if the bass tone is a chord tone, it is an inversion; if not, it is usually a different chord with a different name.

## 10.4 Thoroughbass

Vivaldi and Biber notate their accompaniment as thoroughbass: a bass line with figures giving the intervals above the bass. No figure means a triad in root position, 6 the sixth chord, 6/4 the six-four chord, 7 the seventh chord, 4–3 a suspension of the fourth resolving into the third. A sharp or flat beside a figure alters that tone, a lone accidental the third.

[[c10-figured]]

The example shows a figured bass line and above it a realisation: E without figure is Em; C with 6 is a sixth chord, i.e. Am/C; B with 4–3 is the dominant with a suspended fourth, E resolving to D♯; E without figure is Em again. The harpsichordist or organist realises the chords from this by the rules of voice leading (chapter 12). The chord symbols of rock are the direct descendant of this practice: both give the player the harmony and leave the voicing to them.

## 10.5 Roman numerals with inversions

Roman-numeral analysis marks inversions with appended figures taken from thoroughbass: triad in first inversion 6, in second 6/4; seventh chord in root position 7, in first inversion 6/5, in second 4/3, in third 4/2.

[[c10-roman]]

Am/C is iv6 in E minor, B7/D♯ is V6/5. The example leads i–iv6–V6/5–i with a bass that moves by step, E–C–D♯–E, because the inversions free it from the roots: that is the point of inversion in part writing. A slash between two numerals, by contrast, means reference: V7/iv is the dominant of the subdominant (chapter 13).

## 10.6 Summary

- Seventh chord: triad plus third; the seventh wants to fall by step.
- Five types: 7, maj7, m7, m7♭5, dim7. E Aeolian: Em7 F♯m7♭5 Gmaj7 Am7 Bm7 Cmaj7 D7.
- The minor seventh of the dominant pushes; the major seventh rests.
- add adds without seventh; 9, 11, 13 presuppose the seventh.
- Symbol from left to right: root, quality, seventh, extension, alteration, addition, bass.
- Slash: inversion when the bass is a chord tone; otherwise another chord.
- Thoroughbass and Roman-numeral figures say the same as the symbol: the tones, not the voicing.

c11-tritone.title: The two forces of the dominant: leading tone up, seventh down

c11-full.title: The complete cadence s–D–t: C falls to B, A stays and becomes the seventh

c11-types.title: Authentic, plagal, half cadence, deceptive cadence

c11-phrygian.title: The Phrygian cadence iv6–V and its form in a riff: C5–B5

c11-axis.title: A–D–E–A with leading tone, Em–A–D–Em without

c11-criterion.title: Modal or tonal: Em–C–D–Em runs, Em–C–B7–Em arrives

c11-picardy.title: The same cadence twice: close in minor, close with Picardy third

c11.title: Cadence and function
c11.text:
The cadence is the harmonic close, and whether and how a section closes decides its form of time. This chapter explains the dominant from two tones, introduces the cadence types and draws the line between tonal music, which creates expectation, and modal music, which strings colours. For the repertoire of this book the refusal of the cadence is as important as the cadence itself.

## 11.1 The dominant

The dominant is the chord on the fifth degree. In major it is major by itself; in minor it becomes major through the leading tone of harmonic minor. Its power rests on two tones: the leading tone, which strives a semitone upward into the root of the tonic (D♯ to E), and the seventh, which falls a step into the third of the tonic (A to G). Together they form a tritone, the most unstable interval (chapter 4).

[[c11-tritone]]

Bars 1 and 2 show the force without a chord: the tritone D♯–A contracts inward to the third E–G. Bars 3 and 4 show the same in the chord B7–Em: B stays, D♯ rises, A falls. Without the seventh, B major is a weaker dominant; without the leading tone, as Bm, it is none at all but a modal neighbour.

The subdominant prepares the dominant. Am contains the C that falls to B, and the A that stays and becomes the seventh of B7.

[[c11-full]]

Am–B7–Em is the complete cadence: preparation, tension, release, or in functional letters s–D–t. In the example one sees the path of every voice: A stays for two bars and turns from the fifth of the subdominant into the seventh of the dominant, then falls to G; C falls to B; E rises to D♯ and back to E.

## 11.2 The cadence types

A harmonic close is called a cadence. The authentic cadence leads from dominant to tonic (V–I); it is perfect when both chords are in root position and the melody ends on the root, otherwise imperfect. The plagal cadence leads from subdominant to tonic (IV–I); it has no leading tone and feels soft, like the amen at the end of a hymn. The half cadence ends on the dominant (I–V or IV–V) and leaves the phrase open. The deceptive cadence leads the dominant not to the tonic but to the sixth degree (V–VI, in E minor B7–C); the leading tone resolves upward, the bass moves a step instead of a fourth, and the expected arrival is postponed.

[[c11-types]]

The example shows the four types in turn. Only the first is a complete close; the plagal calms, the half cadence opens, the deceptive extends. The choice of cadence type is the most important decision at the end of a section.

## 11.3 The Phrygian cadence

A special half cadence of the Baroque is the Phrygian cadence: the subdominant in first inversion to the dominant, iv6–V, in E minor Am/C–B. The bass falls a semitone (C–B), the top voice rises a whole tone (A–B), and the close stays open on the dominant. Vivaldi ends slow movements and transitions with it.

[[c11-phrygian]]

Bars 1 and 2 show the Baroque form with contrary motion of the outer voices. Bars 3 and 4 show the same bass motion as power chords: C5–B5, the ending of countless riffs, with an open continuation. The same bass motion, the same openness; only the third is missing.

## 11.4 Modal and tonal

Tonal music creates expectation: every dominant promises the tonic. Modal music strings chords as colours over a centre without a leading tone pushing.

[[c11-axis]]

The example contrasts the two readings of the chain of fourths. Bars 1–4 in A major: D is the subdominant, E with G♯ the dominant, the cadence resolves to A. Bars 5–8 in E minor with almost the same bass: A is the subdominant, D the seventh degree without a leading tone, and E returns like a repetition, not like an arrival. The difference lies in a single third.

[[c11-criterion]]

The criterion is simple: does the chord before the root contain its leading tone? Then tonal. Does it contain the minor seventh of the key (D in E minor) or no third at all? Then modal. Em–C–D–Em can run endlessly; Em–C–B7–Em arrives. The example plays both progressions in turn; one hears how the second pass comes to a halt at the end while the first could keep running.

Vivaldi and Biber are tonal; their sequences are chains of dominants (chapter 14), and almost every phrase cadences. The metal references are predominantly modal; the major dominant appears rarely and then with great effect. Type O Negative, whose harmony stands closer to pop, place real cadences at section endings; My Dying Bride and Anathema mostly end sections by return or break-off.

## 11.5 Refusing the cadence

A section that does not cadence promises nothing, therefore does not disappoint, and can last long. That is the form of time of slow metal: state instead of path. Three forms of refusal: the return to the root without a leading tone (D or Bm before Em), the ending on a chord other than the tonic (the section stops on C or D, the next begins on E), and the break-off (the riff stops, a chord rings out, silence). Expectation arises from leading tone and seventh; without them a chord change is a change of colour, and changes of colour are not urgent.

[[c11-refusal]]

The example plays the same riff with three endings: return without leading tone, ending on D with silence, real cadence with B7 and major tonic. The rule for long pieces: decide per section whether to refuse or resolve, and per piece at most one place where the resolution sits. There it lands with the force of the whole abstention.

[[c11-picardy]]

The major tonic at the end of a minor piece is called the Picardy third. The example plays the cadence Am–B7 twice, once to Em and once to E major: one tone, G♯ instead of G, and the close turns bright. The Baroque closed this way because the pure major third rings out better than the minor (chapter 1); Type O Negative use this close, and in slow metal its impact is larger because it arrives after minutes of minor.

## 11.6 Summary

- The dominant works through leading tone (up) and seventh (down), together a tritone.
- Complete cadence: s–D–t, Am–B7–Em; the subdominant prepares.
- Authentic closes, plagal calms, half cadence opens, deceptive extends.
- Phrygian cadence: iv6–V, bass C–B; in a riff C5–B5.
- Tonal: leading tone before the root. Modal: minor seventh or no third.
- Refusal: return without leading tone, ending on a foreign chord, break-off. Per piece at most one resolution.
- Picardy third: major tonic at the end of a minor piece.

c12-common.title: Four chord changes from Em: common tones stay, the rest takes the shortest path

c12-eight.title: Eight chords in three upper voices with shortest paths

c12-parallels.title: Parallel fifths: avoided in part writing, the purpose of a riff

c12-top.title: D7–G: held top tone, moving inner voices

c12-pedal.title: Pedal point on the tonic and on the dominant beneath changing chords

c12-hands.title: Voice leading under the hand: the thumb stays on E, the little finger on B

c12.title: Voice leading
c12.text:
A chord change is not a change of shape but the motion of individual voices. This chapter states the five rules by which voices move from chord to chord, shows them on chord pairs, on a longer progression and on the instruments, and treats the pedal point as the voice leading of a bass that stands still.

## 12.1 Chords as voices

Four-part writing, in which voice leading is taught, distributes every chord among bass, tenor, alto and soprano; every voice has a line of its own that must be singable by itself. That is the criterion by which every voicing can be measured, whether on the keyboard, in Type O Negative's organ or in Vivaldi's continuo: can every voice be sung on its own?

## 12.2 The basic rules

First: common tones stay in the same voice. Second: the other voices take the shortest path, usually a semitone or whole tone. Third: the bass may leap; it carries the roots and moves in fourths, fifths and thirds while the upper voices almost stand still. Fourth: leading tone and seventh resolve in their direction, the leading tone upward, the seventh downward.

[[c12-common]]

Em to C: E and G stay, B moves to C. Em to Am: E stays, G to A, B to C. Em to B7: B stays, E to D♯, G to F♯. Em to D: no common tone, everything shifts a step downward. In all four bars the bass leaps and the upper voices move by at most a whole tone; that is the division of labour in part writing.

[[c12-eight]]

The example leads eight chords in three upper voices over a leaping bass. The top voice stays on E until D forces it; the largest moves lie where two chords share no tone.

Fifth, from classical writing: two voices should not move in parallel octaves or perfect fifths when they are meant to be heard as independent, because the parallel fuses the two voices into one.

[[c12-parallels]]

Bar 1 shows the parallel fifths E–B to F♯–C♯: both voices take the same path, and the ear hears one voice that has grown thicker. Bar 2 leads the same top voice with contrary motion to F♯–A, and both voices stay audible. Bar 3 shows that in a riff the rule does not apply: E5–G5–A5–B5 are deliberate parallel fifths, and doubling in octaves is their purpose. The rule is not a prescription but a description: parallels fuse. Whoever wants fusion writes them; whoever wants two voices avoids them.

## 12.3 Top voice and inner voices

The top voice is heard most clearly; it is the melody of the chordal writing. Inner voices are perceived as motion, not as line. A good accompaniment keeps the top voice calm and lets the inner voices make the semitone steps.

[[c12-top]]

From D7 to G, D stays on top, F♯ rises to G, C falls to B. In Type O Negative the organ carries this kind of writing, in Anathema the keyboard pad; in both the bass makes the motion, on top one tone changes.

## 12.4 Pedal point

A pedal point is a bass tone that stays while the harmony above it changes. On the tonic it rests; on the dominant it tenses, because every chord above the sustained B pushes toward Em.

[[c12-pedal]]

Bars 1 to 4 hold E beneath Em, C, Am and B7: the sound stays at home even where the chords move away; C over E is Cmaj7/E, B7 over E a tense sound that becomes Em again at once. Bars 5 to 7 hold B beneath Em, Am and B7: every chord over the sustained B is a dominant with additions, and the tension grows until bar 8 falls to E. Vivaldi places dominant pedals before the return of the ritornello; Biber lays a repeated bass model in the ciaconas, a rhythmicised pedal. On the guitar the pedal point is the open string: E, A or D lie without a finger, and above them the writing moves. That is the basis of the modal harmony of this book and the reason the references linger so often on one bass tone.

## 12.5 Voice leading on the instruments

On the keyboard voice leading means not shifting the hand but single fingers.

[[c12-hands]]

From Em to Am the thumb stays on E and the other two fingers each move a step; from Em to B7 the little finger stays on B, and thumb and middle finger move a semitone and a whole tone downward. On the P4 guitar voice leading means leaving one finger down and moving two; where pure fourths allow close positions only with a leap, the writing is spaced wider and the voice leading stays the same. In solo playing over an open bass the upper voices on the middle and high strings are the voices of the writing; each of them should take its own path, otherwise it is a change of shape and not a change of chord.

## 12.6 Summary

- Every voice must be singable by itself; that is the measure of every voicing.
- Common tones stay; the others take the shortest path; the bass may leap.
- Leading tone up, seventh down.
- Parallels fuse voices: avoided in part writing, intended in a riff.
- Top voice calm, inner voices move: the writing of organ and pad.
- Pedal point: tonic rests, dominant tenses; on the guitar it is the open string.

c13-secondary.title: Secondary dominants: E7 → Am, D7 → G, G7 → C, then B7 → Em

c13-v7iv.title: The one secondary dominant of doom: Em becomes E7 before Am

c13-neapolitan.title: The Neapolitan F/A before the dominant, and its core in a riff: F5–E5

c13-symmetry.title: One diminished seventh chord, four names: the octave divided into four equal parts

c13-dim7.title: One diminished seventh chord, four resolutions

c13-pivot.title: Fifth-related modulation from E minor to A minor via the pivot Am

c13-modulation.title: Fifth-related modulation with pivot, third-related change without

c13-shift.title: Third-related shift without pivot: the same riff a minor third higher

c13.title: Extended harmony
c13.text:
Extended harmony adds tones to the key from outside: leading tones to secondary degrees, the lowered second, the symmetrical diminished seventh chord, and finally the change of the centre itself. This chapter shows the Baroque formulas that shape these devices and their path into metal, where they usually appear reduced to their bass.

## 13.1 Secondary dominants

Any major or minor chord of the key can become the tonic for a moment by being preceded by its own dominant. This secondary dominant is a dominant seventh whose root lies a fifth above the target chord, and it usually introduces a tone foreign to the key, the leading tone to the target. In E minor: E7 (with G♯) to Am, A7 (with C♯) to D, D7 to G, G7 (with F) to C, F♯7 (with A♯ and C♯) to B. In analysis one writes V7/iv, V7/VII and so on; the slash here means reference, not bass tone.

[[c13-secondary]]

The example strings three secondary dominants and closes with the real dominant. Without the seventh chords the same root sequence would stay modal; every secondary dominant adds a direction. Vivaldi strings them in falling fifths, each chord the dominant of the next (chapter 14).

[[c13-v7iv]]

In doom secondary dominants are rare because they bring major thirds and direction; the exception is the change from Em to E major before Am, i.e. V7/iv. The example shows it: the third G becomes G♯ for one bar, the seventh D is added, and Am afterwards sounds like an arrival. Power chords cannot render this change because it needs the third; it belongs to the keyboard, the violin or a second guitar in the high register.

## 13.2 The Neapolitan

The Neapolitan sixth chord is the major chord on the lowered second degree, usually in first inversion: in E minor F major with A in the bass, F/A. It stands before the dominant and replaces the subdominant: F/A–B7–Em. The semitone step F–E in the top voice is the same as in Phrygian, but here as a cadence.

[[c13-neapolitan]]

Bars 1 to 3 show the Baroque form: F/A, then B7, in which F falls to D♯, a leap across a diminished third that makes the Neapolitan unmistakable, then Em. Bars 4 and 5 show its core in a riff: F5 before E5, the semitone from above in the bass. Biber uses the Neapolitan in the sarabandes, Vivaldi before half cadences; in a riff it appears as an F5 power chord before the root, since its effect lies in the bass.

[[c13-formulas]]

The example places three Baroque formulas side by side: the Phrygian cadence (chapter 11), the Neapolitan and the dominant pedal over which Em, Am and B7 change before Em arrives. All three stay recognisable as power chords because they are defined in the bass; that is their path into metal.

## 13.3 The diminished seventh chord

D♯dim7 = D♯ F♯ A C consists of three minor thirds and divides the octave into four equal parts.

[[c13-symmetry]]

Therefore every inversion is again a diminished seventh in root position: F♯dim7, Adim7 and Cdim7 contain the same tones, and there are only three different diminished seventh chords in all. The example plays the four inversions; each sounds like a root position because all the distances are equal.

[[c13-dim7]]

Each of the four tones can be a leading tone and resolve a semitone upward: D♯ to E, F♯ to G, A to B♭, C to D♭. A single chord therefore leads into four keys, each a minor third apart. As a dominant substitute, D♯dim7 before Em corresponds to a B7♭9 without root; the sound is sharper than B7 because the tritone is present twice. Vivaldi uses the diminished seventh for storm and terror, often as tremolo; in slow metal it appears in passing (E–D♯–D in the bass) and in organ pads as church sound. The leading-tone dim7 (D♯dim7 to Em) must be distinguished from the dim7 over its own root (Edim7 = E G B♭ D♭), which is a colour over E and not a dominant.

## 13.4 Modulation

A modulation confirms a new centre, as a rule through its own cadence. Fifth-related keys sit next to each other in the circle of fifths and share six of seven tones; the route leads via a shared chord, the pivot, to the dominant of the new key.

[[c13-pivot]]

From E minor to A minor: Am is iv in E minor and i in A minor, the pivot; E7 is the new dominant, with G♯, which does not occur in E minor; Am is the arrival. After the third bar E minor has been left without any jolt being heard. Vivaldi modulates in every fast movement to the dominant or the relative key and back; Biber closes the first part of a dance movement in the dominant or relative and comes home in the second.

Third-related keys lie a third apart and share fewer tones; the change is a jolt. E to C (major third down) opens, E to G (relative) is soft, E to C♯ or E♭ is hard. The chromatic mediant changes between keys of the same mode a third apart, E minor to C minor, with two foreign tones and a cinematic sound.

[[c13-modulation]]

[[c13-shift]]

The metal references often change sections third-related and without pivot, by the bass alone: a riff returns a minor third higher. The example plays a two-bar riff in E minor and then the same figure in G minor, with B♭ instead of B; nothing mediates, the bass starts afresh. That is not modulation in the tonal sense but a shift of weight. Rule: fifth-related for routes meant to lead back; third-related for contrast that may be heard as a break.

## 13.5 Summary

- Secondary dominant: dominant seventh a fifth above the target chord; it brings the target's leading tone.
- In doom what remains is V7/iv: Em becomes E7 before Am.
- Neapolitan: major chord on ♭II, usually as F/A before B7; in a riff F5–E5.
- Diminished seventh: four equal parts, three different chords, four resolutions.
- Fifth-related modulation: pivot, new dominant, arrival. Third-related change: jolt without pivot.
- The riff a minor third higher is a shift of weight, not a modulation.

c14-ascending.title: The ascending tetrachord B–C–D–E: the arrival after the descent

c14.title: Bass models and sequences
c14.text:
A bass model is a fixed bass sequence over which the upper voices move freely; a sequence is the transposition of a pattern to other degrees. Both are the engines of Baroque harmony and, often unrecognised, the building forms of the riff. This chapter presents the most important models: lamento, circle of fifths, chain of sevenths, falling thirds and the ostinato of the ciacona.

## 14.1 The lamento bass

The oldest model in this book is the descending tetrachord from root to fifth, the lamento bass: diatonic E–D–C–B or chromatic E–E♭–D–D♭–C–B. In the 17th century it was the formula of lament; Vivaldi uses it in slow movements, Biber in variations. It works because every step is small, the direction unambiguous and the goal, the dominant, the point of greatest expectation. Over every bass tone a different chord can be built: Em, D (or Bm/D), C, B.

[[c14-lamento]]

The example shows both versions and the arrival on Em. In the chromatic one the upper voices fall in parallel sixths, and every bass step carries a chord of its own.

[[c14-riff]]

Slow metal did not quote the lamento bass but rediscovered it; Em–D–C–B is the progression of countless riffs, mostly in power chords. The example plays it as E5–D5–C5–B5 with a line above that stands in thirds and sixths to the bass and at the end brings on D♯ the leading tone that the power chord B5 itself lacks.

[[c14-ascending]]

The ascending tetrachord B–C–D–E is the reverse of the model and the arrival after the descent: B, C, D, Em, every step a chord, and the last one the tonic. Descent and ascent together form an eight-bar shape that does without a cadence and still arrives.

## 14.2 The circle of fifths

The circle-of-fifths sequence strings roots in falling fifths or rising fourths: E–A–D–G–C–F♯–B–E. In E Aeolian this gives Em–Am–D–G–C–F♯dim–Bm–Em; with a leading tone the last link becomes B major. Each chord is the dominant of the next in terms of bass motion even when it is minor; that is why the sequence creates pull without needing a leading tone. Vivaldi builds whole ritornellos from falling fifths. In a riff two links suffice, Em–Am or D–G; the more links, the stronger the pull and the less modal.

[[c14-fifths]]

The upper voice of the example is itself a sequence: the same three-tone motif is transposed along with the bass. Where the scale has semitones the motif changes its spacing; that is the diatonic sequence which chapter 24 treats as a formal device.

## 14.3 The chain of sevenths

Giving every chord of the circle of fifths a seventh makes it fall into the third of the next chord: D, the seventh of Em7, becomes C, the third of Am7; G, the seventh of Am7, becomes F♯, the third of D7. Two voices alternate, one holds, one falls. That is the engine of the Baroque sequence and the basis of every modulation in Vivaldi.

[[c14-sevenths]]

In slow metal sevenths are rare because they create direction; where they occur they are minor seventh and major seventh chords as colour that do not resolve. The chain of sevenths itself belongs to the Baroque; as a riff it would be too tonal.

## 14.4 Other sequence models

Falling thirds (E–C–A–F♯) are soft because every chord shares two tones with the next; the sequence floats and suits a riff without a goal. Rising fifths (E–B–F♯) are the reverse of falling fifths and build rather than release. Falling seconds are the lamento.

[[c14-thirds]]

Bars 1 to 4 show the falling thirds: from Em to C, E and G stay, from C to Am, C and E stay, from Am to F♯m7♭5, A, C and E stay; the upper voices hardly stir, and the progression could continue in any direction. Bars 5 to 8 show the rising fifths Em–Bm–F♯dim: every step moves away from the centre, and the diminished chord on F♯ forces the return.

Each of these motions can be led diatonically (within the key) or really (with constant semitone spacing, hence modulating).

[[c14-sequence]]

Bars 1 to 4 transpose a motif diatonically downward: the letters shift, the spacings follow the key, and the sequence stays in E minor. Bars 5 to 8 transpose the same motif really, each time exactly a whole tone lower with the same semitone spacings; after three steps, with F, E♭, D♭ and B♭, the key has been left. The diatonic sequence is the rule; the real one is a means of modulation and in the Baroque a sign of intensification.

## 14.5 Ostinato: ciacona and passacaglia

An ostinato is a bass model that repeats unchanged while everything above it changes. The Baroque ciacona (also chaconne) and passacaglia are variation sets over a four- or eight-bar bass in triple meter; Biber closes the third partita of the *Harmonia artificioso-ariosa* with a ciacona and the fifth with a passacaglia. After the second pass the listener knows the bass and hears only what is new above it.

[[c14-ciacona]]

The example lays out a four-bar bass model E–B–C–B in quarters and brings an upper voice with leading tone on the second pass. The model can be repeated any number of times; every pass needs only a new upper voice, and after the last one an ending must stand, otherwise the piece stops instead of ending.

[[c14-layers]]

The riff is the same principle: a bass model repeats, and voice, violin or lead guitar vary above it. The example shows three layers over Em–C–Am–B7: the bass, a figure in eighths that fills it out, and a melody that moves freely above. Chapter 20 treats the layered texture, chapter 25 repetition as form.

## 14.6 Summary

- Lamento: E–D–C–B, diatonic or chromatic; the goal is the dominant. As a riff: E5–D5–C5–B5.
- Ascending tetrachord B–C–D–E: the arrival.
- Circle of fifths: every chord the dominant of the next in the bass; pull without leading tone.
- Chain of sevenths: the seventh falls into the third of the next chord; Baroque, not doom.
- Falling thirds float, rising fifths build, falling seconds lament.
- A diatonic sequence stays in the key; a real one modulates.
- Ostinato: bass unchanged, variation above; ciacona and riff are siblings.

c15.title: Meter and subdivision
c15.text:
Rhythm is the ordering of time into beats and their weighting, meter the grouping of those beats. This chapter leads from the pulse through subdivision to the deviations that make rhythm interesting: syncopation, polyrhythm, hemiola, odd meters, swing. Each of these deviations presupposes that the pulse stays audible; without reference no deviation can be heard.

## 15.1 Pulse and accent

Music orders time into even beats, the pulse, and the pulse orders itself into groups with an accented first beat, the meter. The bar is the notation of meter (chapter 3). There are two basic meters: duple with groups of two or four beats and triple with groups of three. Within a 4/4 bar the first beat is heaviest, the third second heaviest, the second and fourth light.

[[c15-accents]]

Accent arises through loudness, length, harmonic change and bass entry. Bars 1 and 2 make it audible with accent marks; bars 3 and 4 achieve the same without accents, merely because the bass changes on 1 and 3 while the melody stays on one tone. The ear hears the harmonic change as weight. The drums make the same weighting audible with kick and snare (chapter 17).

## 15.2 Binary and ternary

Every beat can be divided in two or in three. Duple division (eighths in 4/4) is the straight, walking feel; triple division (triplets in 4/4 or eighths in 12/8) the rocking one. All further subdivisions are combinations: sixteenths are 2 × 2, sextuplets 2 × 3 or 3 × 2.

[[c15-binary]]

The bass strikes the same quarters in both bars; the upper voice divides them first in two, then in three. The triplet is written with the figure 3 above the group; three triplet eighths last as long as two ordinary eighths. If triple division occurs only occasionally, triplets are written. If it governs the piece, the meter changes: 12/8 is the honest notation of triple with four beats, 6/8 with two, 9/8 with three. The tempo mark then names the dotted quarter.

[[c15-compound]]

The example in 12/8 is counted 1-2-3 2-2-3 3-2-3 4-2-3. The bass holds two big pulses per bar. The same tone sequence in 4/4 as straight eighths would walk instead of rock; the subdivision is not a detail but the basic posture of a piece. Vivaldi writes the Danza pastorale, the third movement of Spring, in 12/8; Type O Negative have pieces in triple meter and in 6/8; My Dying Bride alternate within a piece between straight and triplet riffs.

## 15.3 Syncopation

A syncopation shifts the accent to a light beat or between the beats.

[[c15-sync]]

It arises in three ways: through an entry on the "and" that is held across the next strong beat (bar 1); through a rest on the strong beat so that the first tone comes on the light one (bar 2); through an accent on the light beat in an otherwise straight rhythm (bar 3). The first form is written with a tie so that the beat played across remains visible (chapter 3). The syncopation works only while the pulse stays audible; that is why the bass holds the whole note in every bar. Without reference it is just another rhythm.

## 15.4 Polyrhythm and hemiola

In polyrhythm two voices divide the same span differently: three against two, four against three. The shared span is divided into the least common multiple, for 3:2 into six; the triple voice enters on 1, 3 and 5, the duple voice on 1 and 4. Both share only the beginning.

[[c15-poly]]

The hemiola is a polyrhythm in succession: within a triple bar six eighths are grouped 2+2+2 instead of 3+3, or in two 3/4 bars six quarters as 3+3 instead of 2+2+2. For a moment the bar feels like another one. Vivaldi and Biber place the hemiola before the cadence in almost every triple meter: uniformity breaks, and the arrival gains weight.

[[c15-hemiola]]

[[c15-332]]

In the 4/4 of metal the grouping 3+3+2 of the eighths is the same idea: eight eighths, but the accents come every three, and the bass holds the straight grid of quarters beneath. Bar 3 sets the straight grouping beside it; the difference is solely the position of the accents, the tones are the same. Whoever plays 3+3+2 for two bars and then straight experiences the return of the even bar as an arrival.

## 15.5 Odd meters

An odd meter is a chain of groups of two and three that does not split into equal halves: 5/8 as 2+3 or 3+2, 7/8 as 2+2+3, 3+2+2 or 2+3+2, 5/4 as 3+2 or 2+3 in quarters. The grouping is part of the composition, not of the notation; 2+3 and 3+2 are different rhythms.

[[c15-odd]]

[[c15-five]]

Two uses: as the basic meter of a section, which the listener hears as normal after two bars, or as a single bar in an even surrounding that shortens a riff by an eighth or lengthens it by a quarter. The second use is the more frequent in slow metal: the riff catches once and moves on. An odd meter must come from the phrase; if the grouping cannot be sung, it is wrong.

## 15.6 Swing and shuffle

Swing shifts the second eighth of every beat backward. Straight eighths are written with the indication swing or shuffle, and long–short is played. The ratio varies: 2:1 corresponds to the triplet, 3:1 to dotting, 3:2 lies between; at slow tempo it becomes more extreme, at fast tempo straighter. Drum machines give it as a percentage of the first eighth: 50 straight, 67 triplet, 75 dotted (appendix C). The French Baroque practice of unequal notes (notes inégales) likewise plays written equal eighths unequally; whether a Vivaldi recording does so is a decision of the ensemble. Unequal eighths have been a question of performance, not of notation, for three hundred years.

[[c15-swing]]

The example writes a riff straight and carries the swing indication; the preview plays 2:1. The references of this book hardly swing; the shuffle enters metal via the blues and is here a device for one's own pieces, not a trait of the models.

## 15.7 Summary

- Pulse, meter, bar: beats, their grouping, their notation. In 4/4, 1 is heavy, 3 medium, 2 and 4 light.
- Weight arises through accent, length, harmonic change and bass.
- Binary walks, ternary rocks; lasting triple division is written as 12/8, 6/8, 9/8.
- Syncopation: entry on "and", rest on the beat, accent on the light beat; it needs the audible pulse.
- Polyrhythm divides simultaneously, hemiola in succession; 3+3+2 is the hemiola of 4/4.
- Odd meters are chains of 2 and 3; the grouping must be singable.
- Swing is long–short with straight notation; a device, not a trait of the references.
