c16.title: Tempo and the shaping of time
c16.text:
Tempo is more than a number: it decides how long a tone sounds, how a bar feels and where the boundaries of a piece lie. This chapter treats tempo as a decision about decay, the half-time feel, the freedoms of rubato and fermata, the small shifts of agogics and the relations between two tempi.

## 16.1 Tempo and decay

Tempo is the speed of the pulse, measured in beats per minute (chapter 3).

[[c16-seconds]]

At ♩ = 60 a quarter lasts one second, a half two, a whole four, an eighth half a second. The example plays these values in turn over a bass that holds every whole note; whoever counts along hears how long four seconds on one tone are. For the music of this book tempo is a decision about decay. A clean guitar tone decays noticeably after two to four seconds; a distorted power chord carries six to ten seconds because distortion raises the quiet phases of the decay.

[[c16-decay]]

A chord tied across three bars at ♩ = 60 lasts twelve seconds. Such values are playable distorted and not clean. Conversely at ♩ = 140 with eighths every tone has 0.2 seconds; distortion then only thickens the attack. Fast metal therefore sounds percussive, slow metal pad-like, with the same amplifier. Reverb lengthens further: two seconds of reverberation make every tone half a beat longer at ♩ = 60 and smear the attacks at fast tempo. The churches for which Baroque music was written had several seconds of reverberation; the tempi of the slow movements are built on that. Rule for one's own tempo: the longest note of the piece must be shorter than the sustain of the instrument.

## 16.2 Half-time

The same tempo can feel twice as fast or half as fast depending on where the accent lies.

[[c16-halftime]]

The example writes a drum pattern on the pitched staves (chapter 17): the hi-hat as eighths on top, the snare as an accent in the middle, the kick at the bottom. In bars 1 and 2 the snare lies on 2 and 4; the bar feels in quarters. In bars 3 and 4 it lies only on 3; the bar feels in halves, the half-time feel, although tempo and hi-hat are unchanged. The hi-hat keeps the grid, the snare defines the felt speed.

Slow metal lives on this feel: ♩ = 60 with snare on 3 feels like ♩ = 30 in halves, and a riff of whole notes is a sixteen-second thought. A change from half-time to a straight backbeat at the same tempo feels like a doubling without any tone getting faster; that is the metric modulation of rock.

## 16.3 Rubato, ritardando, fermata

Rubato means stolen time: a phrase is stretched in one place and given back in another so that the pulse survives across the phrase. Ritardando slows gradually, usually into a close; accelerando speeds up. The fermata holds a tone or rest for an indefinite length; time stands still. The Baroque knows less rubato than Romanticism, but cadences are stretched, and slow movements such as the Largo of Winter demand that the solo voice phrase freely over the steady bass. Biber's praeludia contain free passages without fixed meter.

[[c16-rubato]]

Music with drums has no rubato but fermatas: the last chord of a section rings out, the drums drop out, the next riff starts anew. For solo playing without accompaniment rubato is the most important freedom and the greatest danger. Rule: stretch within the phrase, not between phrases; the beginning of every phrase lies on time. Fermatas only at form boundaries and never twice in a row.

## 16.4 Agogics

Agogics is the small deviation from the grid at constant tempo. A tone arriving ten to forty milliseconds after the beat sounds heavy and lies "behind the beat"; one before it pushes. Slow metal lives on laying back: the snare minimally late, the guitar attack minimally behind the kick, the voice behind everything. The ear hears delay as inertia, hence as mass. The Baroque knows the same micro-delay as accent: the good note may be longer than the bad one, the first beat longer than the second, not merely louder.

[[c16-agogic]]

Rule: one element behind the beat, never all. If everything is late, only the tempo is slower. On drum machines the shifting of single hits is called nudge or microtiming; it lies below the sixteenth grid, since a sixteenth itself would already be 250 milliseconds at ♩ = 60 and thus a rhythm, not a weight.

## 16.5 Tempo relations

Two sections can stand in simple ratios: double (♩ = 60 to ♩ = 120), half, or linked through a shared subdivision.

[[c16-ratio]]

The example shows the link through the triplet: at ♩ = 60 a triplet quarter lasts 0.667 seconds; that is exactly the quarter at ♩ = 90. Whoever keeps counting the triplets of the first two bars as new quarters has raised the tempo by half without a break; the preview plays both halves at one tempo so that one hears the note values running at the same speed. Such transitions are possible without a break because one note value stays constant. A free tempo change, by contrast, is a break and is heard as a form boundary. Vivaldi's movements stand in fixed tempi and change only between movements; the metal references change within a piece, mostly through half-time and doubling, rarely through new values.

## 16.6 Summary

- ♩ = 60: a quarter is one second, a whole four; the longest note must be shorter than the sustain.
- Distortion lengthens the decay; that is why slow metal carries whole notes and fast metal only attacks.
- Half-time: snare on 3 halves the felt speed at the same tempo.
- Rubato stretches within the phrase; fermatas only at form boundaries.
- Agogics: one element behind the beat, never all.
- Tempo change without break via a shared note value; free changes are form boundaries.

c17.title: The drums
c17.text:
In this music the drums are less an engine than a grammar: they say where the beat lies, how fast the bar feels and where a section ends. This chapter treats their notation, the three levels of a pattern, the weighting of hits, the form signals and the pattern as a grid, device-neutrally, so that it can be built on any drum machine.

## 17.1 Notation

The drums are written on a staff with a percussion clef in which the lines denote instruments, not pitches: the kick sits in the lowest space, the snare in the third space from the bottom, the hi-hat with cross-shaped noteheads above the staff, the toms on the lines between, cymbals as crosses at the top. Note values apply as elsewhere; rests likewise. This book writes drum examples on the pitched staves of the preview so that they can be heard: the hi-hat as B4, the snare as E4, the kick as E2. The reading is the same as on the percussion staff, three voices with rhythms of their own.

## 17.2 The grammar of a pattern

A pattern has three levels. The hi-hat (or ride) gives the subdivision: quarters, eighths or sixteenths. It is the grid on which everything else hangs; closed it sounds dry, open it is an accent with decay. The snare gives the backbeat: in 4/4 on 2 and 4 or, in half-time, only on 3. The kick gives the foundation and links with the bass: on 1 and 3, or on 1 alone, plus syncopations doubling the rhythm of the bass voice.

[[c17-patterns]]

The example places both basic patterns side by side. The tempo is the same; the snare on 3 halves the felt speed (chapter 16).

[[c17-weight]]

The accents mark the weighting: the kick on 1 is louder than the one on 3, the hi-hat on the beats louder than between them, the snare loudest. Bar 1 plays the pattern without this weighting, bar 2 with it. Without weighting every pattern sounds like a machine; with it even a programmed one sounds played.

[[c17-compound]]

In 12/8 the same grammar applies with groups of three: the hi-hat plays the twelve eighths, the kick lies on the first and third of the four big beats, the snare on the third. That is the half-time of the rocking bar, the pattern of the slow 12/8 riffs.

## 17.3 The drums in slow metal

At tempi between fifty and eighty the drums are less an engine than an architect. The rests are long; one hit every two seconds is normal, and every hit therefore has to sit. Half-time is the default, the kick follows the bass rhythm, toms replace the snare at transitions, the ride replaces the hi-hat in open sections, and the crash rings out long.

[[c17-tremolo]]

The Baroque has no drum kit but the same function: the continuo marks cadences by thickening, the tutti marks the return of the ritornello, and Vivaldi's sixteenth-note tremolo in the bass is the drum kit of the storm. The example shows it: held chords over a bass that strikes every tone sixteen times. The harmony stands still, the motion comes solely from the repetition of the attack.

## 17.4 Fills and form signals

The drums make the form audible. A fill in the last bar before a boundary, a crash on the new one, a change of pattern from half-time to a straight backbeat, a bar without drums before the chorus: each of these signals tells the listener that a section ends. Without signals the form stays inaudible; with them the harmony has less to do.

[[c17-fills]]

At slow tempo two or three tom hits suffice as a fill; a dense roll would betray the tempo.

[[c17-signals]]

Two further signals: in bar 3 the drums drop out, and the silence is louder than any fill; bar 4 re-enters with the crash on the one, and the new section is marked. Both signals cost nothing and work more strongly at slow tempo than at fast, because the pause is longer.

## 17.5 Patterns as grids

Device-neutrally every pattern is a grid of steps, sixteen per 4/4 bar at sixteenth resolution, twelve per 12/8 bar, and per step an instrument with a velocity. Building a pattern means: choose the grid; put the hi-hat on every second or fourth step; the snare on step 9 (half-time) or 5 and 13 (straight); the kick on 1 and on the steps where the bass attacks; weight the velocities, strong on 1 and 9, medium on the beats, soft between; put the fill in the last bar before the boundary on steps 13 to 16 and drop the hi-hat there; swing only if the riff is ternary. Grid, velocity, swing and nudge are the four quantities every drum machine offers under its own names; whoever knows them finds them on any device.

## 17.6 Summary

- Three levels: hi-hat gives the grid, snare the backbeat, kick the foundation with the bass.
- Weighting makes the difference between machine and playing: strong on 1, medium on the beats, soft between.
- Half-time is the default at ♩ = 50–80; in 12/8 the same grammar with groups of three.
- The Baroque has no drum kit but tremolo, tutti and continuo with the same function.
- Form signals: fill, crash on the new one, pattern change, drop-out.
- Pattern as grid: steps, instruments, velocities; the four quantities of every drum machine.

c18-passing.title: Dissonance on light beats: passing and neighbour tone; leaps only into consonances

c18-suspensions.title: The three suspensions 4–3, 7–6 and 9–8: prepared, dissonant on the heavy beat, resolved

c18-thirds.title: Thirds and sixths through E Aeolian

c18-sixths.title: Parallel sixths and their release into contrary motion

c18-bassmelody.title: Bass and melody as two-part writing: pedal, then falling bass against rising melody

c18.title: Two-part writing
c18.text:
Two voices are the smallest texture in which all the rules of polyphony already apply. This chapter treats the types of motion, the handling of consonance and dissonance, the suspension, the parallels in thirds and sixths, imitation and canon, and finally bass and melody as the two-part skeleton of every piece on one instrument.

## 18.1 Types of motion

Two voices can move in four ways relative to each other. Parallel motion: same direction, same interval, such as thirds or sixths. Similar motion: same direction, changing interval. Oblique motion: one voice holds, the other moves; that is the pedal with melody from chapter 12. Contrary motion: opposite directions.

[[c18-motion]]

The mixture keeps two-part writing alive; pure parallels sound like one voice with an effect, pure oblique motion like a drone. With two violins, as in Biber's partitas, the types of motion change within a few bars; with two guitars, as My Dying Bride lead them, parallels in thirds and sixths over the riff dominate, and the violin adds a third voice above.

## 18.2 Consonance and dissonance in part writing

Between two voices, octave, fifth, third and sixth are consonances; second, seventh and tritone dissonances. The fourth is a dissonance against the bass because the bass is heard as the root and the fourth above it sounds like a suspension before the third; between two upper voices over a bass it is a consonance. In strict writing consonances stand on the accented beats; dissonances appear on light beats as passing or neighbour tones reached and left by step, or on heavy beats as suspensions.

[[c18-passing]]

Bar 1: F♯ over C is a tritone, but it stands on the light beat, is reached by step and left by step; that is the passing tone. Bar 2: F♯ over E is a second, circles the G as a neighbour tone and returns. Bar 3: the upper voice leaps G–B–G–E, and every leap lands on a consonance with the lower voice. That is the rule: dissonances are entered and left by step, leaps lead into consonances.

## 18.3 The suspension

A suspension is a tone held over from the previous chord that becomes dissonant in the new one and then resolves downward by step. It has three phases: preparation (the tone is consonant), dissonance (on the heavy beat), resolution (on the light one). The most common suspensions are 4–3 (fourth resolving into third), 7–6 (seventh into sixth) and 9–8 (ninth into octave), named after the intervals above the bass.

[[c18-suspensions]]

The example shows all three in the same form: one bar of preparation, in which the tone lies consonant over its bass, then the bass change that makes the held tone dissonant, then the resolution by a step downward. A over A is the octave; over E it becomes the fourth and resolves to G. B over D is the sixth; over C it becomes the seventh and resolves to A. C over A is the third; over B it becomes the ninth and resolves to B. Vivaldi's Largo movements consist over long stretches of chains of such suspensions; the tension arises not through new chords but through delayed voices. Slow metal does the same when the violin or a keyboard tone holds across a chord change and becomes dissonant for a bar. The first example of this chapter likewise ends with a suspension: A held over E as a fourth resolving to G.

## 18.4 Parallel thirds and sixths

Two voices a third apart through a scale alternate between major and minor thirds: in E Aeolian E–G, F♯–A, A–C and B–D are minor, G–B, C–E and D–F♯ major. Sixths are the inversions: the minor third becomes a major sixth. Thirds sound dense, sixths open; both are the standard parallels of the Baroque between first and second violin, and both are the standard parallels of two guitars.

[[c18-thirds]]

[[c18-sixths]]

Under distortion the rule from chapter 1 applies: parallel thirds in the register above E4 and with less gain than the riff; sixths tolerate more gain because their combination tones lie higher and quieter. Parallels are a colour, not a state; after a few bars the writing calls for contrary motion. The example leads four sixths upward and releases them in the second bar into contrary motion: the upper voice falls D–C–B, the lower rises D–E–G, and the two voices are heard as two again.

## 18.5 Imitation and canon

Imitation means one voice repeating what another played shortly before. In a canon this happens strictly: the second voice (the comes) follows the first (the dux) at a fixed distance and fixed interval, usually the octave or fifth, and the melody must be built so that it stays consonant against itself. Biber's partitas contain canons for two violins; the *Harmonia artificioso-ariosa* is over long stretches a textbook of two-part writing.

[[c18-canon]]

The example is a canon at the octave one bar apart over a sustained E: the descending scale follows itself, and because one voice is always a step ahead, sixths arise continuously, Biber's favourite parallel. At the end the following voice resolves via F♯ to G and closes with the third.

## 18.6 Bass and melody as two-part writing

On a guitar alone or in two hands every piece with bass and melody is two-part writing.

[[c18-bassmelody]]

Bars 1 and 2 show oblique motion over an open bass, the default; bars 3 and 4 contrary motion with falling bass E–D–C–B and rising melody G–A–B–D♯, the climax; bar 5 the arrival. The rules of this chapter apply there unchanged: consonance on the heavy beat, dissonance prepared and resolved, every voice singable on its own. Parallels are the colour between.

## 18.7 Summary

- Four types of motion: parallel, similar, oblique, contrary; the mixture makes the texture.
- Consonances on heavy beats; dissonances as passing or neighbour tones on light beats, entered and left by step.
- Suspension: preparation, dissonance on the heavy beat, resolution downward; 4–3, 7–6, 9–8.
- Thirds dense, sixths open; under gain thirds high, sixths more robust.
- Canon: a melody against itself, consonant at a fixed distance.
- Bass and melody are two-part writing; contrary motion is the climax.

c19-target.title: A melody with target tone over a descending bass

c19-phrases.title: Two phrases, two breaths, one target tone

c19-overpower.title: Melody over power chords: the line decides the mode

c19-characteristic.title: Pentatonic plus characteristic tone: first neutral, then Aeolian, then Phrygian

c19-roles.title: The three bass roles: doubling, foundation, countervoice

c19-register.title: Who owns the bass range: guitar and bass equally low, or the bass alone

c19.title: Melody and bass
c19.text:
Melody and bass are the two outer voices a listener perceives first. This chapter treats melody as contour, phrase and goal, its relation to power chords, and the bass in its three roles and its register. What lies between, the layers and pads, is treated in chapter 20.

## 19.1 Motif and contour

A melody is a sequence of tones with its own contour, rhythm and goal. Its smallest building block is the motif: two to five tones with a rhythm, recognised as a unit. The contour is the outline of the motion, rising, falling, arched, static; it is recognised even when the pitches change, and is therefore what links a sequence or a variation to the original (chapter 24).

[[c19-contour]]

Four bars from the same tones of the Em triad: rising, falling, as an arch, and as a leap with stepwise return. Steps (seconds) hold the line together, leaps (a third and larger) open it; after a large leap a good melody usually returns by step in the opposite direction, as in bar 4 after the leap E–B.

## 19.2 Target tone and phrase

Every phrase has a tone toward which it runs: the target tone, usually at the end, often the root or the fifth, in modal music also the characteristic tone. What the target is, is decided by duration, accent and position at the phrase end.

[[c19-target]]

The example leads a melody in half notes over a descending bass. Its goal is the semitone step D♯–F♯ at the end, which the bass prepares with B; everything before is the way.

[[c19-phrases]]

Between two phrases the melody breathes: a rest or a long tone separates them. The example has two two-bar phrases, each with a rest at the end, and a target tone in the fifth bar on which both arrive. Slow metal has long phrases with few tones; the rests are often longer than the phrases. The violin in My Dying Bride and the voice in Anathema lead such lines over the riffs; Vivaldi's solo violin has shorter phrases with more tones, but the same principle: motion to the goal, then breath.

## 19.3 Melody over power chords

Over fifths without thirds the melody determines the mode of the chord.

[[c19-overpower]]

A G over E5 makes the sound minor, a G♯ major. In this music the melody therefore carries the harmony the accompaniment lacks. The usual material is the pentatonic (chapter 6) because all its tones are consonant over the root; bars 3 and 4 show a pentatonic phrase that would sound right over every power chord of the key.

[[c19-characteristic]]

The full scale adds the characteristic tones: ♭6 (C) makes the mode Aeolian, ♭2 (F) Phrygian. The example begins pentatonic, neutral, and then colours with one semitone step each. A pentatonic solo sounds right over every power chord of the key; a modal solo sounds better over the right power chord.

## 19.4 The three roles of the bass

The bass has three possible jobs. As doubling it plays the guitar riff an octave lower: pressure and unity, no new information; that is the default in doom. As foundation it plays roots in long values under chords or figures: calm and room for the motion above; that is the default in Anathema and in every continuo. As countervoice it has a line of its own with passing tones, leaps and rhythm: two-part writing and density; Type O Negative often let the bass carry the actual melody under the voice.

[[c19-roles]]

[[c19-continuo]]

The Baroque continuo unites foundation and countervoice: the cellist plays roots on the heavy beats and passing tones between, and the bass is the score from which the harpsichordist reads the chords. The example shows such a bass under Em–Am–B7–Em: the one carries the root each time, the quarters between move by step to the next. Rule: the bass changes less often than the melody or as often, never more often. When the bass is busier than the upper voice, the register tips over.

## 19.5 Bass register

The bass owns the range from about 60 to 250 Hz, E1 to B3. What sounds there at the same time competes.

[[c19-register]]

Bar 1 places the guitar fifth in the bass range, E2–B2, where the bass plays; bar 2 sets the guitar an octave above and leaves the E2 to the bass alone. Slow metal decides per album who owns this range: the low guitar doubled by the bass, or the bass alone with the guitar above. Nobody lets two instruments be equally strong in this range. For solo playing register is the distribution of the voices: bass low, melody high, inner voice between, and the minor third never below C3 (chapter 1). The kick drum sits below the bass at 50 to 80 Hz and shares space with it, not with the guitar.

## 19.6 Summary

- Motif: two to five tones with rhythm; the contour stays recognisable when pitches change.
- Steps bind, leaps open; after a leap, back by step.
- Every phrase has a target tone and then breath; in slow metal the rest is often longer than the phrase.
- Over power chords the melody decides the mode; the pentatonic is neutral, characteristic tones colour.
- Three bass roles: doubling, foundation, countervoice; the continuo unites the last two.
- The bass never changes more often than the melody. The bass range belongs to one instrument.

c20-registers.title: Layering by register: fifth, organ with third, vocal line

c20-density.title: A density arc: build to the maximum, silence, single tone, wind-down

c20.title: Layered writing
c20.text:
A complete texture is more than bass and melody: between them lie figures, pads and inner voices, and every layer needs its rhythm and its register. This chapter treats the three layers, the arpeggio figure, the distribution by register, density as a controllable quantity, the frequency spaces of the sounds and the question of what happens in an instrumental piece with the register of the voice.

## 20.1 Three layers

A complete texture has three layers with different tasks: the bass sets the reference, a middle voice or figure keeps the motion, and long tones above form the melody. The layers differ in rhythm, not only in pitch: the bass changes rarely, the figure runs in eighths, the melody has few long tones with rests.

[[c20-three]]

The example shows all three over Em–C–Am–B7: wholes in the bass, eighths in the figure, halves with rests in the melody. Every layer is recognisable on its own because it has its own rhythm. Two layers with the same rhythm are one layer.

## 20.2 The arpeggio figure

An arpeggio distributes the tones of a chord in time. As a middle layer it supplies motion without melody; the figure stays the same while the bass changes, and only the tones that do not fit the new chord move a step. So the texture stays calm although it moves. On *Eternity* Anathema build long sections from clean arpeggio figures over keyboard pads; Vivaldi's accompanying voices break chords into even motion in a similar way.

[[c20-arpeggio]]

The example holds E and E′ as common tones across all changes and adapts one tone per change. Five rules for long sections of this kind: the bass changes at most every four bars. The figure stays, the tones adapt. The melody has rests longer than its phrases. One tone stays across the whole section. Density rises only once, at the end.

## 20.3 Register and layering

Every layer needs its range. The foundation lies below C3, the riff between E2 and E4, pads and inner voices between G4 and C6, the line above or between where it is free. On *October Rust* this layering is especially clear: the guitar in B standard carries fifths in the low register, the keyboards the thirds above, the voice sits low and is doubled an octave higher, and the bass is wide and doubles the guitar. Nothing overlaps.

[[c20-registers]]

The example builds the stack in three steps: fifth, organ with third from G4, vocal line between. If the organ sat an octave lower, the third would move into the range of the guitar's combination tones (chapter 1).

## 20.4 Density

Density has four dimensions: the number of voices, the number of attacks per bar, the width of the register and the sonic density through gain, reverb and chorus. Each can be controlled separately. A section with one voice, many attacks, narrow register and heavy gain is dense in a different way from one with four voices, few attacks, wide register and a clean sound. Across a piece density can be drawn as a curve; typically in slow metal voices and register grow until the last quarter while attacks stay low, with a drop in the middle. Vivaldi's ritornello form yields a zigzag: tutti dense, solo thin, with rising peaks.

[[c20-density]]

[[c20-terrace]]

Dynamics without a knob: loud is relative. Two bars of a single voice before the full texture make it louder than any knob could. The example shows the terraced dynamics of the Baroque, in which tutti and solo alternate, and the drop before the riff in metal, both the same thing. A crescendo exists in both only as growth in voices, one after another. Rule: per piece one maximum of all four dimensions, and it does not lie at the beginning; per piece one minimum, and it does not lie at the end.

## 20.5 Frequency spaces

What register is for the voices, frequency space is for the sounds. Sub-bass 20–60 Hz, bass 60–250, low mids 250–500, mids 500–2000, highs above. Every source has a fundamental range and an overtone range; a distorted guitar fills the space from 80 Hz to 4 kHz almost completely. Two sources equally loud in the same range mask each other. Tools: a high-pass on everything that is not foundation; a low-pass on the distortion above 6 to 8 kHz; a narrow cut where two sources collide.

[[c20-stack]]

The example layers bass, guitar fifth, pad and line so that each layer has its range. With a high-pass on pad and line the foundation stays clear; without it the pad masks the guitar's overtones.

## 20.6 The gap of the voice

Four of the five references have vocals, and they occupy the mids between E3 and A4. Instrumental music must decide what happens in this register.

[[c20-gap]]

Bars 1 and 2 leave the register free: bass below, pad above, air between, and the gap is the sound. Bars 3 and 4 occupy it with a line, on guitar on the middle strings, on the keyboard around C4, or as a synthesizer, just as in Vivaldi the solo violin occupies the soprano register. What does not work is filling the register with chords: chords in E3–E4 are the riff register; they make density, not melody. A line needs a voice, not a block.

## 20.7 Summary

- Three layers: bass sets the reference, figure keeps the motion, melody lies above; each with its own rhythm.
- Arpeggio figure: stays the same, adapts one tone per chord; common tones hold through.
- Register: foundation below C3, riff E2–E4, pads G4–C6, line where free; nothing overlaps.
- Density has four dimensions; one maximum, one minimum per piece, not at the beginning and not at the end.
- Terraced dynamics: loud is relative to the silence before.
- Frequency spaces: high-pass on everything that is not foundation.
- The register of the voice: leave it free or occupy it with a line, never fill it with chords.

c21.title: Guitar and amplifier
c21.text:
The guitar with its amplifier is one instrument, not two; the distortion is part of the sound, and with it the rules of part writing change. This chapter treats the types of distortion, the signal chain, sustain as the basis of tempo, the modulation effects, harmonics and bending, and string tension at low tuning.

## 21.1 Types of distortion

Distortion is clipping (chapter 1), and its kinds differ in how hard the waveform is cut. Overdrive rounds the peaks softly, like an overdriven tube preamp; it responds to the attack, and played softly it stays nearly clean. Distortion cuts hard, compresses more strongly and sounds even regardless of attack. Fuzz cuts extremely and brings the waveform close to a square; it is the sound of early doom and turns muddy quickly on chords. High gain chains several stages of distortion and is heavily compressed. With every level the combination tones grow, and with them the number of tolerable intervals shrinks.

[[c21-gain]]

The example places in every bar a triad with third and a power chord without third side by side. Clean, the third is usable and the sustain short; with overdrive the third stays usable and the sustain grows; with distortion the third turns rough and the power chord carries long; with fuzz the third is noise and the power chord a wall.

[[c21-intervals]]

From this follows a mapping: clean tolerates the close third in low position; overdrive demands the third as a tenth, an octave further away; distortion demands the power chord below and the third high in another voice; fuzz tolerates only the power chord. Two gain levels for every rig, one for thirds and one for power chords, and they are not the same. The reference albums work with medium gain; none with fuzz or high gain, since both would bury the thirds and sixths of the second guitar and the keyboards.

## 21.2 Gain staging

The guitar's signal chain is a series of levels: pickup, pedals, preamp, effects loop, power amp, speaker. At every stage the level must be such that the next neither hisses nor distorts unintentionally. Distortion belongs before the effects loop; delay, reverb and chorus belong after it, otherwise the repeats are distorted too and smear. A compressor before the distortion lengthens the sustain and smooths the attack; it is the tool for clean arpeggios. After the distortion it is redundant, because distortion already compresses. The input levels of the effects units are set so that the loudest chord stays just below the clipping point.

## 21.3 Sustain

How long a tone carries depends on gain, register and instrument. Clean, E2 sounds audibly for about four seconds, E4 two; with high gain E2 ten, E4 six. Reverb adds its decay time.

[[c21-sustain]]

The example translates this into note values at ♩ = 60: the distorted low tone carries two tied wholes, eight seconds; the clean high tone has died away after a half, two seconds, and a quarter is the honest spelling for what is still audible afterwards. These figures determine the slowest sensible tempo (chapter 16): the sustain in seconds divided by four gives the duration of a quarter for whole notes. A table for one's own rig, clean, medium and high gain, each for E2, E3 and E4, is the basis of every tempo decision.

## 21.4 Chorus, flanger, phaser

All three are short, modulated delays mixed with the original. Chorus delays by 15 to 35 milliseconds and modulates the time slowly; the result hovers like two slightly detuned instruments. Flanger delays by 1 to 10 milliseconds with feedback; the result is a comb filter sweeping through the spectrum. Phaser does not delay but shifts phases in all-pass filters; notches sweep without beating. Type O Negative put chorus on bass and guitar; the sound widens without an instrument being added, and that is why *October Rust* sounds full with few instruments.

[[c21-modfx]]

Rule for chorus on distorted guitar: after the distortion, slow (around 0.3 Hz), little depth, and a high-pass on the effect signal so the fundamental stays dry and only the overtones hover. Without the high-pass the foundation blurs.

## 21.5 Harmonics and bending

A natural harmonic arises when the string is touched at a node and plucked: above the twelfth fret the second partial sounds (the octave), above the seventh the third (octave plus fifth), above the fifth the fourth (two octaves), above the fourth the fifth (two octaves plus major third). The diamond notehead denotes the sounding tone.

[[c21-harmonics]]

The example shows the four common harmonics on the E and on the A string. On the E string they give E3, B3, E4 and G♯4, on the A string A3, E4, A4 and C♯5: partials 2 to 5 of the string, octave, octave plus fifth, double octave and double octave plus major third, the overtone series from chapter 1. Harmonics are pure tones with few overtones and therefore tolerate much gain; they give solo playing a second register above the open strings.

Bending pulls the fretted string sideways and raises the pitch continuously, usually by a semitone or whole tone to a heard target tone. The arrow in the notation names the target. Vibrato is a small, repeated bend; it raises the pitch and returns, it does not swing symmetrically around the fretted tone.

[[c21-bending]]

The intonation of a bend is checked against the target tone, which is heard fretted beforehand; in the example A4 is the fretted tone and B4 the target.

## 21.6 Low tuning and strings

Tuning lower reduces string tension with the square of the frequency (appendix A). A fourth lower at the same gauge means 56 percent of the tension; the string buzzes on the frets and intonates poorly. Heavier strings restore the tension. Type O Negative's guitar in B standard therefore needs a heavy set; the P4 guitar with C4 and F4 instead of B3 and E4 needs a semitone more tension on the two high strings, which common sets tolerate.

## 21.7 Summary

- Overdrive rounds, distortion cuts, fuzz squares; with every level the tolerable intervals shrink.
- Clean: close third. Overdrive: tenth. Distortion: power chord plus high third. Fuzz: power chord.
- Distortion before the effects loop, time and space effects after it; compressor only before the distortion.
- Sustain determines the slowest tempo: seconds divided by four gives the quarter.
- Chorus, flanger, phaser are short modulated delays; chorus on gain only with a high-pass.
- Harmonics: frets 12, 7, 5, 4 give octave, fifth, double octave, major third.
- Low tuning needs heavier strings; tension falls with the square of the frequency.

c22.title: Synthesizers
c22.text:
In this music the synthesizer is not merely a piano substitute but the carrier of the thirds, the pads and the bells that the guitar cannot supply under gain. This chapter explains subtractive synthesis, wavetable and FM, modulation, the three keyboard roles of the references and the consequences of the held tone for the writing. It names no instruments; the parameters are called similarly everywhere, and the mapping is a matter of the respective manual.

## 22.1 Subtractive synthesis

A subtractive synthesizer produces a harmonically rich signal and removes overtones from it with filters. The chain: oscillator, filter, amplifier, each controlled by envelopes and LFOs. The oscillator supplies the waveform: sawtooth with all partials, bright, the basis for strings; square with odd partials, hollow; triangle with odd partials at 1/n², soft; sine with only the fundamental. Two oscillators detuned against each other by five to fifteen cents give beating and width: the basis of every pad. The pulse width of a square changes its spectrum, and an LFO on the pulse width is the classic string sound.

The filter: a low-pass lets everything below the cutoff frequency pass; resonance emphasises the cutoff. 24 dB per octave cuts steeply and warm, 12 dB gently and open. The high-pass removes lows and is indispensable for pads over a guitar; the band-pass lets a band through and sounds nasal.

The envelope shapes the course: attack is the time to the maximum, decay the time to the sustain level, sustain the held level, release the time to silence after the key is let go. An envelope on the amplifier shapes loudness, one on the filter the timbral course. A pad has an attack around one second and a release around two; an organ attack zero, full sustain and short release; a bass attack zero and short decay.

[[c22-waveforms]]

The example shows the same chord as it is conceived with four sounds: a sawtooth with open filter, a square, a triangle, and two detuned sawtooths with slow envelope and high-pass as a pad. The piano preview plays the tones; the sounds arise at the instrument.

## 22.2 Wavetable and FM

A wavetable oscillator has, instead of a fixed waveform, a table of many waveforms; one parameter selects the current one, and if it is modulated by envelope or LFO the sound travels through the table. This gives spectral motion that a filter alone cannot supply: metallic, glassy, vowel-like. For pads that change over seconds this is the sound of wavetable synthesis.

Frequency modulation lets one oscillator modulate the pitch of another so fast that new overtones arise. Integer frequency ratios (1:1, 2:1, 3:1) give harmonic spectra, fractional ones (1:1.41) inharmonic; the modulation depth determines brightness. Bells, electric pianos and metallic basses are FM sounds. The bells on *October Rust* belong to this family.

[[c22-wavetable]]

## 22.3 Modulation

Sound design is largely the choice of connections between sources and destinations: velocity to the filter (hitting harder makes brighter), modulation wheel to the wave position, LFO to the pulse width, envelope to the filter (opens on attack and closes), key position to the filter (high notes brighter). Synthesizers lead these connections either in a modulation matrix, a list of source, destination and amount, or as a morph, in which wheel, velocity or pedal move almost every knob between two stored settings; the names change from instrument to instrument, the principle does not.

## 22.4 The three keyboard roles

Three sounds cover what the keyboards of the references do. The organ: square or stacked sines, attack zero, full sustain, short release, little filtering, plus a slow modulation in the manner of the rotating speaker; it carries the third and does not move, the church sound of Type O Negative.

[[c22-organ]]

The example shows the organ's writing over power chords: the guitar plays E5, C5, A5, B5 without thirds, the organ lies above from G4 and supplies the thirds G, E, C and D♯; from chord to chord it changes one tone. So the sound stays clean below and complete above (chapters 9 and 12).

The string pad: two to three detuned sawtooths, pulse-width modulation, low-pass around two kilohertz, high-pass around 150 hertz, attack under a second, release over one, chorus and reverb; it fills the gaps between the guitar chords in My Dying Bride and Anathema. The choir: like the pad but with a band-pass around 800 hertz or vowel waveforms and a long attack; a voice without words in the register above C5.

[[c22-pad]]

The high-pass is a register decision, and the example writes it out: bar 1 places the pad in the register of the riff, E3 to B3, where it masks the guitar's overtones; bar 2 places the same tones from G4, where they stand free. What the filter removes at the instrument, the voicing anticipates on paper.

[[c22-roles]]

Rule: one keyboard sound per section, two only in separate registers. The piano stays unprogrammed; in My Dying Bride it stands alone with the violin, in Type O Negative it opens pieces and disappears.

## 22.5 Synthesizers in the texture

A synthesizer holds a tone as long as desired; a piano lets it decay. Both are right, but it changes the writing.

[[c22-hold]]

Over a held synth bass the rest has to be written, otherwise it does not occur; over a piano bass it occurs by itself. The example plays the same line twice: first over a bass that holds through two bars, then over one that is silent every second half note. The line is the same, the texture is not. Pads need the high-pass, otherwise they mask the foundation (chapter 20). And sounds with a long release demand slow tempo, for the same reason as the distorted guitar.

## 22.6 Summary

- Subtractive: oscillator, filter, amplifier; envelopes and LFOs control. Two detuned oscillators are the basis of every pad.
- Sawtooth bright, square hollow, triangle soft, sine pure; low-pass 24 dB warm, 12 dB open; high-pass for everything above the guitar.
- Wavetable moves the spectrum; FM produces bells and metal.
- Modulation is the connection of source and destination; matrix or morph, the principle is the same.
- Three roles: organ carries the third, pad fills the gaps, choir sings above C5. One sound per section.
- The held tone demands written rests; a long release demands slow tempo.

c23.title: Delay and reverb
c23.text:
Delay and reverb are the time effects: they repeat and lengthen what was played, and thereby change the writing, not only the sound. This chapter treats the four parameters of delay, the delay time in the bar, the three delay types, the parameters of reverb and the question of which register reverb belongs to.

## 23.1 The four parameters of delay

A delay stores the signal and plays it back later. Four parameters determine everything. The time: below 30 milliseconds no repeat is heard but doubling; 30 to 100 is slapback, a single short echo; 100 to 500 is rhythmic delay, audible in time; above that spatial effect. The feedback: the share of the output fed back into the input; zero gives one echo, 30 to 50 percent three to five audible repeats, above 70 a long tail. The filter: every repeat is filtered; a low-pass darkens the echoes and lets them recede behind the original, a high-pass keeps the bass clean. The modulation: an LFO on the time creates pitch wobble in the repeats, slight as warmth, strong as chorus.

## 23.2 Delay in time

The delay time follows from the tempo: 60000 divided by the beats per minute gives the quarter in milliseconds. At ♩ = 60 the quarter is 1000, the eighth 500, the dotted eighth 750, the eighth triplet 333. Appendix C holds the table. A dotted-eighth delay over eighth notes produces a sixteenth pattern because every repeat lands a sixteenth before the next attack; a quarter delay over half notes doubles the attacks; an eighth-triplet delay over straight eighths produces shuffle.

[[c23-time]]

The example writes out what the delay does: bar 2 shows the first repeat of a dotted-eighth delay over the arpeggio of bar 1 as sixteenths, bar 4 the quarter delay over the held chord of bar 3 as four attacks.

[[c23-fill]]

On clean guitar the delay fills the gaps between the arpeggio tones; that is its task in Anathema. The example plays an arpeggio in which every second eighth is a rest, and then the same with an eighth delay without feedback: every rest is filled by the repeat of the previous tone, and four attacks per bar become eight without the hand doing more. On distorted riffs the delay is redundant because the signal is already dense.

## 23.3 Tape, BBD, digital

Three technologies, three sounds. The tape echo records the signal to tape and reads it back delayed; every repeat loses highs, the tape wobbles slightly in pitch, and it saturates at high level: warm, blurred, the repeats merge. The bucket-brigade delay (BBD) passes the signal along a chain of capacitors; it loses highs strongly, modulates by itself and has short maximum times: dark, dense, behind the original. The digital delay copies exactly: clear, present, the repeats compete with the original. The four parameters cover everything: tape is medium time, moderate low-pass, slight modulation, saturation; BBD is strong low-pass, built-in modulation, short time; digital is everything off.

[[c23-types]]

The discrimination test listens to the third repeat: with tape darker and slightly wobbling, with BBD almost only mids, with digital identical to the original. Digital effect units emulate tape and BBD from the same building blocks: low-pass and high-pass in the feedback path, slow modulation of the delay time, light saturation; whoever knows the three blocks can build any delay type on any unit.

## 23.4 Reverb

Reverb is the sum of thousands of reflections. Its parameters: the pre-delay, the time to the first reflection, which makes the room larger and the original clearer; the decay time until inaudibility; the damping of the highs, which die earlier than the lows in real rooms; the diffusion, the density of reflections. A high-pass on the reverb signal keeps the bass range clean and is the most important setting for this music. The types: room, short and natural; hall, long, concert hall or church; plate, dense and bright without room feel; spring, the spring reverb of the guitar amplifier.

[[c23-tail]]

The reverb tail is a duration, and the example writes it as a note value: at ♩ = 60 two seconds of reverb are a half note. Bars 1 and 2 play a half and leave the following half to the reverb; the staccato half stands for the decay that is not struck. Bars 3 and 4 play whole notes, and the reverb reaches into the middle of the next tone. Whoever composes with reverb counts the decay as part of the note; otherwise two tones stand where one is written.

## 23.5 Reverb as a register decision

Reverb lengthens tones and fills registers. On the foundation, bass and low guitar, it has no business; on line and pad, violin, pad and lead guitar, it may be long; on the riff a short room remains. Vivaldi and Biber were played in churches and halls whose reverberation is part of the sound; the tempi of the slow movements are built on it. In slow metal the violin carries long reverb and the riff hardly any; the organ reverberates, the bass stays dry.

[[c23-room]]

The example places a riff with rests and a high line with rests side by side. With a short room the riff's rests stay audible; with a long hall they are filled, and the riff loses its edges. For the line the reverse holds: the reverb carries the tones across the rests. In solo playing without a band reverb is the only second instrument; it belongs on top.

## 23.6 Summary

- Delay: time, feedback, filter, modulation; every delay sound is contained in them.
- Delay time from tempo: 60000 divided by BPM is the quarter in milliseconds.
- Dotted eighth over eighths gives sixteenths; an eighth delay fills rests; on gain delay is redundant.
- Tape: loss of highs, wobble, saturation. BBD: dark, short. Digital: exact.
- Reverb: pre-delay, decay time, damping, diffusion; a high-pass on the reverb is mandatory.
- The reverb tail is a duration; at ♩ = 60 two seconds are a half note.
- Reverb belongs on top: line and pad long, riff short, foundation dry.

c24-motif.title: A motif, its repetition and two variations that each change one property

c24-treatments.title: One motif and three treatments: sequence, inversion, augmentation

c24-retrograde.title: Two further treatments: retrograde and diminution

c24-period.title: An eight-bar period: antecedent with half cadence, consequent with full close

c24-sentence.title: The sentence as phrase form: basic idea, sequence, continuation with fragmentation, cadence

c24-lengths.title: Four bars as the measure of expectation and a fifth that breaks it

c24-riff.title: A riff as motif with bass and its augmentation: the same tones in doubled values

c24.title: Motif, phrase, period
c24.text:
Form begins in the small: with the motif that is recognised, with the phrase that breathes, and with the period in which two phrases answer each other. This chapter introduces the treatments by which long pieces arise from few motifs, and shows the two basic forms of the phrase, period and sentence, plus the measure of the eight-bar unit and the riff as motif with bass.

## 24.1 The motif

The motif is the smallest unit recognised as an idea: a few tones with a rhythm. It is defined not by its pitches but by the union of contour and rhythm; that is why it stays recognisable when transposed, mirrored or stretched. A piece needs few motifs. What makes it long is their treatment.

[[c24-motif]]

Repetition is the simplest treatment and the basis of all others; without it there is no reference against which a change could be heard. Variation changes exactly one property and leaves the others standing: in bar 3 it is the rhythm, in bar 4 the final tone. Change two properties at once and the motif is no longer heard as the same.

## 24.2 Treatment

The sequence transposes the motif to another degree, usually a step lower or higher, and keeps contour and rhythm; led diatonically the semitone spacings change in the process (chapter 14). Inversion mirrors the contour: up becomes down. Augmentation doubles the note values.

[[c24-treatments]]

The example leads a three-tone motif through sequence, inversion and augmentation over an E pedal. The references work with the same means: Vivaldi's episodes are sequences of the ritornello motif, Biber's variations are diminutions and embellishments of the aria, and a riff that sounds longer the second time is an augmentation.

[[c24-retrograde]]

Retrograde reads the motif backwards; it is hard to recognise by ear and more a device of writing than of listening. Diminution halves the note values and is the counterpart of augmentation; it turns a motif in quarters into a figure in eighths that fits twice into the bar.

## 24.3 Phrase and period

A phrase is a musical clause with its own breath, usually two or four bars, ending on a cadence or a resting point. Two phrases answering each other form a period: the antecedent ends open, usually in a half cadence on the dominant, the consequent begins alike and ends closed on the tonic. Question and answer, eight bars, and at the end the listener knows that something is complete.

[[c24-period]]

The period is the basic form of the tonal melody; Vivaldi's themes and Biber's dance movements are built from periods. A related form is the sentence: a two-bar motif, its repetition or sequence, then four bars of continuation to the cadence, likewise eight bars, but with acceleration instead of answer.

[[c24-sentence]]

The example shows the sentence: the basic idea over Em, the same idea a fourth higher over Am, then the continuation, in which the motif is shortened to its first two tones and driven over C and B7, finally the cadence. The period answers, the sentence presses; both are eight bars long.

## 24.4 Eight-bar units and riff lengths

The group of four is the measure of expectation: four bars feel complete, eight doubly so, sixteen as a section. Slow metal uses this measure and stretches it: a riff of four bars runs four times, sixteen bars, and only then is heard as a unit.

[[c24-lengths]]

Deviations are devices: the example plays a four-bar riff twice and on the second pass appends a fifth bar on D5 before E5 returns. The listener who expects the return after four bars is held back by a bar; the return weighs more afterwards. Vivaldi's odd phrase lengths in the solo passages and the riff lengthened by a bar are the same technique.

## 24.5 The motif in the riff

A riff is a motif with bass: one to four bars that repeat, with their own contour, rhythm and bass motion. It is treated like any motif, only more slowly: the sequence transposes it a minor third higher (chapter 13), the augmentation lets it appear in halves instead of quarters the second time, the variation changes the last bar.

[[c24-riff]]

The example plays a one-bar riff in quarters twice and then its augmentation in halves across two bars; the guitar fifth above lies still. What carries a riff is its repetition; what develops it is treatment by the rules of this chapter.

## 24.6 Summary

- Motif: a few tones with rhythm; contour and rhythm make it recognisable, not the pitches.
- Repetition is the basis; variation changes one property.
- Sequence transposes, inversion mirrors, retrograde reads backwards, augmentation stretches, diminution shortens.
- Period: antecedent open, consequent closed. Sentence: idea, sequence, continuation, cadence.
- Four bars are the measure; a fifth bar is a device.
- The riff is a motif with bass and is treated like one, only more slowly.

c25-song.title: A miniature song form: A open, B as chorus

c25-repeat.title: Repeat signs as form notation: A twice, then B

c25-ritornello.title: Ritornello form: R, episode, R shortened, episode, R complete

c25-long.title: A long form in miniature: riff A, riff B, break, A in another texture

c25-commontone.title: Transition over a common tone: B stays, the bass changes the section

c25-frame.title: Intro, riff, dropout, new section, outro as frame

c25.title: Repetition as form
c25.text:
Form arises from return and contrast. This chapter orders the three kinds of return, ostinato, ritornello and chorus, sets song form against riff form, explains Vivaldi's ritornello form, names the tools of long form and treats the edges of a piece: intro, outro, transition.

## 25.1 Three kinds of return

Three kinds of return govern the repertoire of this book. The ostinato repeats a bass model unchanged while everything above it changes; Biber's ciacona and the riff are its forms (chapter 14). The ritornello is a section that returns between episodes, often shortened or in another key; Vivaldi's fast movements are built this way. The chorus is the return of a section with words; the song is its form. All three answer the same question: how long may something stay the same? The ostinato very long, if something moves above it; the ritornello only briefly, but often; the chorus so often that one can sing along.

## 25.2 Song form and riff form

Song form orders sections by function: verse (open, narrating), chorus (closed, repeated, denser), bridge (contrast, once), framed by intro and outro. Riff form orders sections as riffs: riff 1 four times, riff 2 four times, riff 1 shortened, riff 3 at a new tempo, riff 2 as the ending. No chorus, but return; the form lives on the contrast between riffs and on the length of the repetitions. *October Rust* is a song album with long intros and outros; *Turn Loose the Swans* builds pieces of seven to twelve minutes from few riffs, each long enough to become a state; *Eternity* mixes both, song form with riff lengths.

[[c25-song]]

The example is a song form in miniature: A open on the pedal, B higher, harmonically moving, with a closing note. What makes B the chorus is register, bass change and close. The same eight bars as riff form, A four times and then B four times, carry longer because every idea gets time to become a state; the song form carries shorter and sticks faster. Without vocals riff form is the natural path; an instrumental chorus needs a motif as strong as a lyric.

[[c25-repeat]]

The repeat signs from chapter 3 are the notation of this form: A stands once on paper and is played twice, then B follows. In the score of a riff piece there are as few bars as there are riffs, and the form stands in the signs.

## 25.3 Ritornello form

A Vivaldi movement begins with the ritornello in the tutti, then follows an episode of the soloist, then the ritornello in the dominant or relative key, often shortened, then another episode, and so on until the complete ritornello in the home key at the end. Four to five ritornellos, three to four episodes. The first ritornello must be complete so that the shortened returns stay recognisable; the last is complete again.

[[c25-ritornello]]

Transferred to the riff: a riff returns between free sections, slightly different each time, and is the anchor that holds the episodes together. That is the form of My Dying Bride's long pieces, without anybody calling it that.

## 25.4 Long forms

What holds a ten-minute piece together is not a chorus but a web. Six tools: riff lengths, every riff runs long enough to become a state, at ♩ = 60 at least four times eight bars. Few riffs, five to seven per piece. Return, at least one riff comes back after a long absence, often in another texture. A break, a section that refuses everything else, silence, piano only, another tempo. Build at the end, the densest point lies in the last quarter. And no ending by cadence but by thinning or breaking off (chapter 11).

[[c25-long]]

The test against arbitrariness: can every riff justify why it stands where it stands? If two sections are interchangeable, one is superfluous. And: what returns? Without return it is a succession, not a piece.

## 25.5 Contrast and density arc

Contrast needs reference: something is only dark if something before was bright, only loud if something before was quiet. The density of a piece (chapter 20) can be planned as an arc: per piece one maximum, not at the beginning, and one minimum, not at the end, and the minimum immediately before the maximum. Two bars of silence before the full riff are the strongest dynamics possible without a knob. Vivaldi builds the arc as a zigzag of tutti and solo, slow metal as a rise with one drop.

## 25.6 Intro, outro, transition

The intro sets key, tempo, sound and expectation: the riff without drums, a foreign instrument alone, a free sound without pulse, or the full riff at once. The outro ends: by thinning, by return of the intro as a frame, by breaking off on a chord. A fade-out is recording technique, not a formal device.

[[c25-commontone]]

The transitions between sections are form parts of their own with their own tools: the fill (chapter 17), the dropout, the overlap of a sustained pad, the common tone across the boundary, the tempo modulation from half-time into quarters. The example shows the common tone: B lies over Em and stays while the bass changes to G and begins the new section; only afterwards does the upper voice move. A transition succeeds when the listener notices the boundary but does not stumble.

[[c25-frame]]

## 25.7 Summary

- Three returns: ostinato (bass stays), ritornello (section returns between episodes), chorus (section with words).
- Song form orders by function, riff form by riffs; without vocals riff form is natural.
- Ritornello form: first and last ritornello complete, between them shortened and in other keys.
- Long form: long riffs, few riffs, return, break, late build, ending without cadence.
- Density arc: minimum immediately before the maximum.
- Transitions are form parts: fill, dropout, overlap, common tone, tempo modulation.

c26-sarabande.title: A sarabande in E minor with emphasis on the second beat

c26-gigue.title: Gigue: fast compound meter with dotted rhythms

c26.title: Suite, variation, programme
c26.text:
The large forms of the Baroque, suite, variation and concerto, and programme music are the models for pieces longer than a song. This chapter presents them through Biber's partitas and Vivaldi's Seasons, shows the dance movements as shapes of time, variation as treatment of a whole theme and the programme as a formal aid, and ends with the album and the concert programme as a suite on a higher level.

## 26.1 The suite

A suite is a sequence of dance movements in one key. Biber's *Harmonia artificioso-ariosa* consists of seven such partitas. Each begins with a free movement, praeludium, sonata or intrada, and then strings dances: allamande, sarabande, gigue, aria, balletto, trezza, canario, amener, plus as finales a ciacona in the third and a passacaglia in the fifth partita; the sixth partita is an aria with thirteen variations, the seventh for two violas d'amore ends with a varied arietta. Every movement type has a fixed character through meter, tempo and rhythm.

[[c26-allemande]]

The allamande stands in duple meter, moderate, with an upbeat and running eighths; the example writes the upbeat as two eighths at the end of an otherwise empty first bar.

[[c26-sarabande]]

The sarabande stands in triple meter, slow, with weight on the second beat: the second beat is long, and there the weight lies. The same eight bars as a gigue in 12/8 at double tempo would be another movement without a single tone changing.

[[c26-gigue]]

The gigue stands in a fast compound meter with dotted rhythms, quarter and eighth within every group of three. The principle of the suite is contrast by type, not by material: one key, many shapes of time. Slow metal does the reverse, one shape of time over many harmonies.

## 26.2 Variation

A variation set presents a theme, the aria, and repeats it with one new treatment each time: the melody embellished in smaller values, the rhythm dotted, the harmony kept or changed, the register changed, the voices swapped. The bass or the harmony remains the constant against which the variation is measured; in the ciacona it is the bass alone (chapter 14), in the aria with variations harmony and phrase structure. Biber's sixth partita shows the set in thirteen stages.

[[c26-aria]]

The example presents a four-bar aria and varies it twice over the same bass: first as embellishment in eighths, then in dotted rhythm. The contour stays recognisable; that is the condition of every variation.

[[c26-variations]]

Two further stages: the third variation moves the aria up an octave without changing a tone; the fourth swaps the voices, the aria goes into the bass, and the upper voice holds what was previously the bass. Transferred to the riff: the bass stays, the texture changes from power chords to arpeggios to single voices, and the form arises from the succession of these versions.

## 26.3 Programme

Vivaldi attached sonnets to the *Four Seasons* and wrote their lines at the corresponding places in the score: birdsong, the murmuring brook, the summer thunderstorm, the autumn hunt, the chattering of teeth in the icy wind of winter.

[[c26-programme]]

The music depicts the images with simple figures: trills for the birds, rocking eighths for the brook, tremolos in the bass for the thunderstorm, repeated tones for the cold; the example sets four of them side by side. The programme gives the form its reasons: the listener knows why a section arrives, and the composer has a reason for every contrast. The metal references are programme music too, with lyrics instead of sonnets. An instrumental piece can have a silent programme, a scene only its author knows; it is not an interpretation but a formal aid: whoever knows which section is the thunderstorm knows how dense, how loud and how long it must be.

## 26.4 The concerto

A Vivaldi concerto has three movements, fast, slow, fast, and the Seasons stand in E major, G minor, F major and F minor. The fast movements are ritornello forms (chapter 25), the slow movements are lines over a sustained accompaniment: in Winter a solo violin over plucked strings, an image of rain on the window. The same three-part shape carries many long pieces of slow metal: a fast or dense frame, a slow, thin middle section, the return. It is the simplest large form with contrast and return.

## 26.5 Album and set as suite

An album or a concert programme is a form on a higher level with the same rules: contrast, density arc, late climax, frame. Biber's suite is the model: one key, different shapes of time. Keys neighbouring in the circle of fifths (E, A, D) flow into one another; a leap of a third is a break and belongs in the middle. Two slow pieces in a row are an intention or a mistake. A forty-minute programme is five to six pieces of this music.

## 26.6 Summary

- Suite: one key, many shapes of time; allamande duple with upbeat, sarabande slow on 2, gigue fast and dotted.
- Variation: theme plus one treatment each; bass or harmony stays the constant.
- Four ways of variation: embellishment, dotting, register, swapped voices.
- Programme: figures depict images and give the form its reasons; a silent programme helps instrumentally too.
- Concerto: fast, slow, fast; the simplest large form with contrast and return.
- Album and set follow the rules of the suite: neighbouring keys flow, leaps of a third break.

c27-mdb.title: The texture of My Dying Bride in miniature: power-chord riff, two guitars in thirds above E4, violin on top

c27-ton.title: The texture of Type O Negative in miniature: fifths below, organ thirds above, a real cadence with major close

c27-anathema.title: The texture of Anathema in miniature: clean arpeggio figure with ninth over a sustained pad and slow bass

c27-vivaldi.title: Vivaldi in miniature: a ritornello head in E major from broken triads with cadence IV–V–I

c27-biber.title: Biber in miniature: two violins in imitation over a continuo bass in D minor

c27-common.title: Eight bars in which all the shared features of the five references come together

c27.title: The five references
c27.text:
The five references of this book are two metal albums from England, one from New York and two Baroque collections from Venice and Salzburg. This chapter describes each with the documented facts of its line-up, tuning and form, shows its texture in one short example each in the style of this book, and names at the end what they share and what they do not. The examples are not quotations but models: they show the mechanism, not the passage.

## 27.1 My Dying Bride, *Turn Loose the Swans* (1993)

The second album of the band from Halifax was released in October 1993 on Peaceville. Line-up: Aaron Stainthorpe (vocals), Andrew Craighan and Calvin Robertshaw (guitars), Adrian Jackson (bass), Rick Miah (drums), Martin Powell (violin and keyboards). Seven pieces, together almost an hour; the longest, *The Crown of Sympathy*, lasts over twelve minutes, three others between nine and ten. The first and the last piece dispense with the band line-up: *Sear Me MCMXCIII* consists of voice, keyboard and violin, *Black God* of keyboard, violin and two voices. On this album the violin is fully integrated into the band's sound, and the vocals combine guttural voice, speech and clear melody.

[[c27-mdb]]

What the book has learned from it: the half-time riff of power chords in low position (chapters 9 and 17), two guitars in thirds and sixths above it, in the register above E4 and with less gain (chapters 1 and 18), the violin as third voice in the soprano register (chapter 19), pieces from few long riffs with return and break instead of cadence (chapters 11 and 25), and the framing by movements without guitar. The example builds the texture in three steps: riff, thirds, violin.

## 27.2 Type O Negative, *October Rust* (1996)

The fourth album of the band from Brooklyn was released in August 1996 on Roadrunner. Line-up: Peter Steele (vocals, bass), Kenny Hickey (guitar, vocals), Josh Silver (keyboards, programming, vocals), Johnny Kelly (drums, on the album as drum machine); the drum tracks are programmed, and Josh Silver, who produced the album with Steele, programmed them. The guitar stands in B standard, a fourth below normal tuning (chapter 7). The album is a song album with ballads, long intros and outros, a cover of Neil Young's *Cinnamon Girl* and two short joke pieces at the beginning.

[[c27-ton]]

What the book has learned from it: the layering by register, fifths below in the low guitar, thirds above in the organ, the voice low and doubled at the octave (chapters 20 and 22); chorus on bass and guitar as width without an additional instrument (chapter 21); real cadences and the Picardy third at section endings, a harmony closer to pop than to modal doom (chapter 11); and the proof that programmed drums carry a slow album when they are weighted (chapter 17). The example closes with the major tonic.

## 27.3 Anathema, *Eternity* (1996)

The third album of the band from Liverpool was released in November 1996 on Peaceville. Line-up: Vincent Cavanagh (vocals, guitar), Daniel Cavanagh (guitar, keyboards), Duncan Patterson (bass), John Douglas (drums), plus guests with vocals, keyboards and, on the cover of Roy Harper's *Hope*, Harper himself with spoken word. The album moves away from the death-doom of the first two albums, with markedly more keyboards and mostly clean vocals.

[[c27-anathema]]

What the book has learned from it: the clean arpeggio figure over a sustained pad as middle layer (chapter 20), chords with ninth and major seventh as colours without direction (chapter 10), the delay that fills the gaps of the figure (chapter 23), song form with riff lengths (chapter 25), and the union of metal dynamics with the calm of a pad that changes over seconds (chapter 22). The example holds E and B as common tones over Emadd9 and Cmaj9.

## 27.4 Vivaldi, *Le quattro stagioni* (1725)

The four concertos for violin, strings and continuo were published in 1725 in Amsterdam as the first four of the twelve concertos *Il cimento dell'armonia e dell'inventione*, opus 8. Spring stands in E major, Summer in G minor, Autumn in F major, Winter in F minor; each has three movements, fast, slow, fast, and each is accompanied by a sonnet whose lines stand at the corresponding places in the score. The fast movements are ritornello forms, the slow ones lines over a sustained accompaniment. The accompaniment is written as thoroughbass.

[[c27-vivaldi]]

What the book has learned from it: the ritornello form as return with episodes (chapter 25), the sequence and the circle of fifths as engine (chapter 14), the cadence as the arrival almost every phrase has (chapter 11), the tremolo as the drum kit of the Baroque (chapter 17), the hemiola before the cadence (chapter 15), the programme as the reason for every contrast (chapter 26), and the suspension chains of the slow movements (chapter 18). The example is a ritornello head in E major, the key of Spring: broken triads over I and V, then the cadence IV–V–I.

## 27.5 Biber, *Harmonia artificioso-ariosa* (1696)

The collection of seven partitas was published in 1696. Five are for two violins and continuo, the fourth for violin and viola, the seventh for two violas d'amore; six of the seven demand scordatura, only the sixth in D major stands in normal tuning (chapter 7, appendix A). Every partita begins with a free movement and then strings dances; the third ends with a ciacona, the fifth with a passacaglia, the sixth consists of an aria with thirteen variations and finale, the seventh ends with a varied arietta.

[[c27-biber]]

What the book has learned from it: two-part writing with imitation, parallels and contrary motion (chapter 18), the ostinato of ciacona and passacaglia (chapter 14), variation as form (chapter 26), the suite as a sequence of shapes of time in one key (chapter 26), and tuning as a compositional device (chapter 7). The example lets a second violin follow the first one bar later, an octave lower, over a bass that prepares the leading tone C♯ on the dominant.

## 27.6 What the five share and what they do not

They share ten features, and these are the grammar of this book: a foundation that changes less often than the line; minor as base colour with ♭6 as characteristic tone; motion in fourths and fifths in the bass, E–A–D, falling fifths, lamento; repetition as form, riff, ostinato, ritornello; contrast through register and density, not through tempo; long tones, wholes and halves as normal values; two-part writing in thirds, sixths and contrary motion over the foundation; one clear climax per piece, late; the tuning of the instrument as a compositional device, scordatura, B standard, P4; and a sound space in which every role has its register.

[[c27-common]]

The example brings all ten together in eight bars: slowly changing bass in thirds and fourths, minor with C, repetition of the motif, held inner voice, long values, late climax with the only cadence in the last two bars.

Not shared, hence a choice: the cadence (Vivaldi always, My Dying Bride almost never), the tempo (Vivaldi's fast movements well above a hundred, doom between fifty and eighty), the gain (the metal albums yes, the Baroque no, but the sustain goal is the same), the form (suite, ritornello, riff, song), the voice (four have it, one does not), the programme (Vivaldi explicit, the bands through lyrics, Biber none). The common denominator is not a style but an attitude to time: it may be long because the foundation carries. Vivaldi and doom share the pedal point, the sequence, the descending bass; they differ in the rate of repetition and in resolution. Type O Negative are the bridge: cadences from pop at Sabbath tempo with church organ. Anathema are the way out of metal with the same harmony.

## 27.7 Summary

- *Turn Loose the Swans*: two guitars, violin, long riffs, frames without band; half-time and thirds above.
- *October Rust*: B standard, programmed drums, organ thirds over fifths, chorus, real cadences.
- *Eternity*: clean figures, pads, chords with ninth, song form with riff lengths.
- *Le quattro stagioni*: ritornello form, sequence, cadence, programme, thoroughbass.
- *Harmonia artificioso-ariosa*: two-part writing, scordatura, ciacona, variation, suite.
- Shared: the foundation carries, time may be long. Different: cadence, tempo, gain, form, voice, programme.
