c28.title: Listening, analysing, writing
c28.text:
Theory is the ability to hear with names. This last chapter applies the book: how to listen to a piece so that one knows what happens in it; how to analyse it so that one can write it down; and how to write, document and, over years, collect one's own pieces into a repertoire with the same terms. It is not a section of exercises but a description of the practice in which the terms of the previous chapters have their place.

## 28.1 Listening

In listening an order applies that follows the construction of this music: rhythm before pitch, bass before melody. First tempo and meter: where is the one, does the snare lie on 2 and 4 or on 3, is the subdivision binary or ternary (chapters 15 to 17)? Then the bass: which roots, how often do they change, in which intervals do they move, is there a pedal, a bass model, a sequence (chapters 12 and 14)? Only then the harmony above the bass: power chord or triad, minor or major, is there a dominant with leading tone or only colours over the centre (chapters 8 to 11)? Finally the melody: its contour, its phrases, its target tone (chapter 19). Whoever hears the melody first hears the piece like a listener; whoever hears the bass first hears it like its author.

Two listening tests from the previous chapters always remain valid: if the chord before the root contains its leading tone, the passage is tonal, otherwise modal (chapter 11). And: if every voice can be sung on its own, it is part writing, otherwise a change of shape (chapter 12).

## 28.2 Analysing

An analysis is a notation of what was heard with the signs of this book. Four levels suffice: the form as a chain of letters with bar counts (A 8, B 8, A′ 8, break 4, A 16); the bass as a tone sequence with durations; the harmony as degrees above the bass, Roman for triads, with 5 for power chords; the layers with their registers and rhythms. In addition, where it applies, the cadence types at section endings, the refusals (chapter 11), the form signals of the drums (chapter 17) and the density arc (chapter 20).

[[c28-analysis]]

The example shows such an analysis on an eight-bar riff: form letters above the bars, degrees above the chords. The second pass is A′ because a single chord is different, the F5 on ♭II, the Phrygian move that carries the close. An analysis is finished when it answers what returns, what changes and why the piece ends where it ends.

The five references are the practice material of this method. With Vivaldi and Biber the score is available, and the analysis compares what is heard with what is written; with the three albums there is no score, and the analysis is the only notation of these pieces there will ever be.

## 28.3 Writing: the working path

A piece arises in seven steps, in this order, each with a verifiable result. First the motif: three to five tones with rhythm, singable, written down (chapter 24). Second the foundation: the bass route for eight to sixteen bars beneath the motif, the mode fixed (chapters 6 and 14); the bass alone must already yield a form. Third the form plan: chain of letters with bar counts, tempo, density arc, break, climax, cadence yes or no (chapter 25); the plan must be readable without notes. Fourth the sketch: every section in bass and line, without inner voices, without sound (chapters 18 and 19). Fifth inner voices and textures: where three layers, where arpeggio, where chord, where gap (chapter 20); every voice singable on its own. Sixth the sound: timbres, effects, frequency plan, drums (chapters 21 to 23, 17). Seventh score and recording.

[[c28-workflow]]

The example leads the same motif four times, each time with one layer more: alone, with bass, with held inner voice, with the inner voice as eighth-note texture. Every stage has its test: motif singable, bass alone a form, inner voice singable on its own, texture without loss of the line. The order is the point: sound before form yields presets without a piece, inner voices before foundation chords without bass. Whoever notices at step five that step three was wrong goes back. Backwards is allowed, skipping is not.

The references worked as bands in the rehearsal room, but their result can be read this way: with My Dying Bride the riff, steps one and two at once, is the core; with Type O Negative the song, step three, comes early; with Anathema the texture, steps five and six. Vivaldi had step three as a convention, the ritornello form, and did not need to plan it.

## 28.4 Roles from one hand

Whoever works alone has two paths: solo playing, in which one instrument carries foundation, inner voice and line, or layered recording, in which every role is recorded separately. The second needs planning because one layer cannot adapt to the next. Order: first drums or click, the grid; then the bass, the foundation; then the rhythm guitar, which listens to the bass; then the pad, which fills the registers; finally the line, which listens to everything.

[[c28-roles]]

Every role has its rhythm: the bass holds, the guitar strikes, the pad lies, the line breathes. Two roles with the same rhythm are one role; that is allowed, but a decision. Every role has rests; a layer that never falls silent is a carpet, not an instrument. What layered recording cannot do is react; the substitute is a second pass in which the earlier layer is adjusted, and a deliberate decision about the agogics of every layer (chapter 16), because they do not arise by themselves. *October Rust* is a studio album with programmed drums and many layers; solo playing remains the test of whether the piece carries alone, layering is the publication.

## 28.5 Rules of one's own

A style is a set of decisions one does not make anew every time. The references have such rules, mostly unwritten: B standard and chorus on everything, half-time and two guitars in thirds, pads and clean figures. Rules of one's own arise from four sources: the instrument (what the rig does well becomes a rule; what it cannot do becomes an exclusion), the references (which of the choices from chapter 27 one takes), the ear (what has proven fitting in listening) and the limits (what one has recognised as a break).

[[c28-rules]]

The form of a rule: short, testable, with an exception. The example sets five of them into bars: the bass changes at most every two bars (bars 1 to 4); thirds only above C5 (bar 2); every phrase has a rest (bar 3); a tone stays across the bass change (bars 4 and 5); a break before the close (bar 7). Rules are not shackles but time saved: whoever knows that the bass stays calm need not think about the bass and can think about the line. They are revisable; a piece that breaks a rule and is better changes the rule. Ten to fifteen rules suffice.

## 28.6 Documenting

A recording is not the piece; it is a performance. The piece is the score plus the sound documentation. Reproducible means: playable the same way in a year with the same means, and approximable for someone else with theirs. Five parts: the score with clef, key signature, meter, tempo unit, all voices, form signs and position marks (chapters 2 and 3); the sound sheet, per role instrument, sound parameters in general terms, effects with the four delay parameters and the reverb type, gain level, frequency plan (chapters 21 to 23); the drum grid with steps, velocities, swing and nudge (chapter 17); the recording log with date, order of layers, tempo and reference take; the deviations, where the recording departs from the score and why.

[[c28-document]]

The example is a complete document in miniature: key, tempo, chords and the form sign Fine stand in the score; the sound sheet for it would be a text of a few lines. Score as sheet music, sound sheet as text, drums as grid, not buried in a project format that cannot be opened in five years. Vivaldi and Biber exist as scores, and every recording is a reading; the three albums exist only as recordings. For one's own pieces both should exist.

## 28.7 Repertoire and set

A repertoire is a set of pieces one can play at any time, not those one once could. Every piece has a state: new, active, resting, archived; a resting piece is active again after a day of practice. A piece exists in versions: solo, layered, shortened, in another key, say moved from E to A; every version is a decision of its own about what the piece is at its core.

[[c28-set]]

A set is a form on a higher level with the same rules as a piece: contrast, density arc, late climax, frame (chapters 25 and 26). The example shows a set in four bars: E calm, A denser and fifth-related, C as a break at the distance of a third, E as climax and frame. Keys neighbouring in the circle of fifths flow; a leap of a third is a break and belongs in the middle. A forty-minute set is five to six pieces of this music; the suite (chapter 26) is the Baroque model for it, and an album is a recorded set.

## 28.8 A practice without a market

Whoever pursues this music without income pursues a practice with a public. Three components: the work, the pieces and their documents; the rhythm, when something gets finished; the public, who hears it. The deadline is the device amateurs usually lack and that costs nothing: one piece per quarter, documented and recorded, regardless of whether it is the best; one set per year, played through. Public means: a recording that someone hears is published. A page with recordings and scores, a performance for two people, a piece sent to someone who understands it. The feedback of a few who listen is worth more than any reach.

Development: revise the rulebook yearly, break one rule deliberately in one piece per year, every few years a new tool, a technique, a form, and check the references: are they still the same? The measure is not whether someone buys it but whether one still wants to play it in ten years. Vivaldi's concertos were long forgotten before they became among the most heard pieces in the world; *Turn Loose the Swans* is over thirty years old and is still heard. That is no guarantee, but the only measure that counts.

## 28.9 Summary

- Listening: rhythm before pitch, bass before melody; leading-tone test for tonal or modal, singability test for part writing.
- Analysing: form as letters with bar counts, bass, degrees, layers; finished when return, change and ending are explained.
- Writing: motif, foundation, form plan, sketch, inner voices, sound, score; backwards allowed, skipping not.
- Roles: bass holds, guitar strikes, pad lies, line breathes; each with rests.
- Rules: short, testable, with exception; ten to fifteen.
- Document: score, sound sheet, drum grid, log, deviations.
- Repertoire and set: states, versions, arc; one piece per quarter, one set per year.

cA.title: Acoustics and tuning
cA.text:
This appendix collects the numbers behind chapters 1, 7 and 21: frequencies, cents, overtones, fret distances, string tension and the tunings of all instruments of this book.

## A.1 Frequency from MIDI number

f = 440 · 2^((n − 69) / 12). A4 = MIDI 69 = 440 Hz. C4 = 60. Every octave doubles; every semitone multiplies by 2^(1/12) ≈ 1.05946.

## A.2 Frequency table (equal temperament, A4 = 440 Hz), rounded



- E1 41.2 · A1 55.0 · D2 73.4 · G2 98.0 · C3 130.8 · F3 174.6
- E2 82.4 · A2 110.0 · D3 146.8 · G3 196.0 · C4 261.6 · F4 349.2
- E3 164.8 · A3 220.0 · D4 293.7 · G4 392.0 · C5 523.3 · F5 698.5
- E4 329.6 · A4 440.0 · D5 587.3 · G5 784.0 · C6 1046.5 · F6 1396.9
- E5 659.3 · A5 880.0 · D6 1174.7 · B0 30.9 · B1 61.7 · B2 123.5
- B3 246.9 · B4 493.9 · B5 987.8 · F#2 92.5 · F#3 185.0 · F#4 370.0
- G#2 103.8 · G#3 207.7 · G#4 415.3 · C#3 138.6 · C#4 277.2 · C#5 554.4
- D#3 155.6 · D#4 311.1 · D#5 622.3 · Eb2 77.8 · Db3 138.6 · Bb2 116.5

## A.3 Cents

1 cent = 1/100 semitone. Distance between two frequencies in cents: c = 1200 · log2(f2 / f1). Pure fifth 3:2 = 701.96 cents, tempered 700 (2 cents too small). Pure major third 5:4 = 386.3, tempered 400 (14 cents too wide). Pure minor third 6:5 = 315.6, tempered 300 (16 cents too narrow). Seventh partial 7:4 = 968.8, tempered minor seventh 1000 (31 cents difference). Pitch discrimination threshold about 5 cents; beating audible from about 1 Hz difference.

## A.4 Overtone series

Partial n has frequency n · f. Over E2 (82.4 Hz): 1 E2 · 2 E3 · 3 B3 · 4 E4 · 5 G#4 (−14 cents) · 6 B4 · 7 D5 (−31 cents) · 8 E5 · 9 F#5 · 10 G#5 · 11 between A5 and A#5 · 12 B5. Harmonic over fret 12 = partial 2, fret 7 (and 19) = partial 3, fret 5 (and 24) = partial 4, fret 4 (and 9, 16) = partial 5, fret 3.2 = partial 6.

## A.5 Fret calculation

With scale length L (nut to bridge) fret n sits at d = L · (1 − 2^(−n/12)) from the nut. For L = 648 mm (25.5 in): fret 1 36.4 · fret 2 70.7 · fret 3 103.1 · fret 4 133.7 · fret 5 162.5 · fret 7 215.5 · fret 9 262.7 · fret 12 324.0 · fret 24 486.0 mm. Fret 12 halves the string. The distance between frets shrinks by a factor of 0.9439 per fret.

## A.6 Intonation

Pressing down stretches the string and raises the pitch; therefore the saddle is set slightly longer than the calculated scale (compensation, 1–4 mm, more for thicker strings). Control: harmonic above fret 12 against the fretted tone at fret 12; if the fretted tone is sharp, the string is lengthened at the saddle.

## A.7 String tension

T = 4 · L² · f² · μ (μ = mass per length). A fourth lower (E → B) lowers f to 0.749; T falls to 0.561. To keep the same tension μ must rise by a factor of 1.78, the diameter by √1.78 ≈ 1.33. A .046 becomes about .061. P4 (C4 F4 instead of B3 E4): the two high strings one semitone higher; tension rises by a factor of 1.12; unproblematic at .009/.011, with heavier sets choose one step thinner.

## A.8 Tunings

Standard E2 A2 D3 G3 B3 E4 (intervals 5-5-5-4-5 semitones). P4 E2 A2 D3 G3 C4 F4 (5-5-5-5-5). Type O Negative B1 E2 A2 D3 F#3 B3: standard a fourth lower, Kenny Hickey consistently in B standard. Bass E1 A1 D2 G2. Violin G3 D4 A4 E5 (fifths). Biber, *Harmonia artificioso-ariosa*, scordaturas per IMSLP: Partia I (D minor) both violins A3 E4 A4 D5; II (B minor) B3 F#4 B4 D5; III (A major) A3 E4 A4 E5; IV (E-flat major) violin Bb3 Eb4 Bb4 Eb5, viola Eb3 Bb3 Eb4 Bb4; V (G minor) G3 D4 A4 D5; VI (D major) normal tuning; VII (C minor) two violas d'amore C3 G3 C4 Eb4 G4 C5. The notation shows fingerings, not sounding pitches. Partia I is a fifth-fourth-fourth chain, the violas d'amore a broken C minor chord: the tuning is the chord.

## A.9 Sustain measurement

Strike the tone, stopwatch, time until audible tipping into noise or until −40 dB on a level meter. One table per rig and register; chapter 21 explains why it determines the tempo.

cB.title: Distortion and intermodulation
cB.text:
This appendix works through the combination tones of chapter 1 completely and derives from them the rules of distorted part writing.

## B.1 Clipping

An overdriven amplifier cuts off the peaks. Soft clipping (tube, overdrive) rounds, producing mainly odd and quiet even overtones. Hard clipping (diode, distortion) produces stronger and higher overtones up to a square wave (fuzz). Every single tone gets overtones at 2f, 3f, 4f …; that is the "brightness" of distortion.

## B.2 Intermodulation

Two tones f1 < f2 produce combination tones: difference f2 − f1, sum f1 + f2, and higher orders 2f1 − f2, 2f2 − f1, 3f1 − 2f2 … The stronger the clipping, the louder the higher orders. All combination tones are real frequencies in the output signal; they are not an auditory illusion.

## B.3 Table over E3 (164.8 Hz)

Interval · upper tone · difference tone · nearest tone · second order 2f1 − f2 · nearest tone. Deviations above 10 cents are in brackets.

- Octave E4 329.6 · diff 164.8 ≈ E3 · 2f1−f2 none
- Fifth B3 246.9 · diff 82.1 ≈ E2 · 2f1−f2 82.7 ≈ E2
- Fourth A3 220.0 · diff 55.2 ≈ A1 · 2f1−f2 109.6 ≈ A2
- Major third G#3 207.6 · diff 42.8 ≈ F1 (−33 cents) · 2f1−f2 122.0 ≈ B2 (−21 cents)
- Minor third G3 196.0 · diff 31.2 ≈ B0 (+18 cents) · 2f1−f2 133.6 ≈ C3 (+37 cents)
- Major second F#3 185.0 · diff 20.2 ≈ E0 (−36 cents) · 2f1−f2 144.6 ≈ D3 (−26 cents)
- Minor second F3 174.6 · diff 9.8 (below hearing: beating, roughness) · 2f1−f2 155.0 ≈ D#3
- Tritone A#3 233.1 · diff 68.3 ≈ C#2 (−26 cents) · 2f1−f2 96.5 ≈ G2 (−26 cents)
- Minor sixth C4 261.6 · diff 96.8 ≈ G2 (−21 cents) · 2f1−f2 68.0 ≈ C#2 (−33 cents)
- Major sixth C#4 277.2 · diff 112.4 ≈ A2 (+37 cents) · 2f1−f2 52.4 ≈ G#1 (+18 cents)

## B.4 Reading

Octave, fifth, fourth: all combination tones are chord tones or their octaves. Major third: the difference tone lies near the root E1 but two thirds of a semitone too high, because the tempered third is 14 cents too wide; the second order lies near B2, the fifth. Viable at medium gain, with audible beating. Minor third: the difference tone lies below the bass at B0, the second order near C3: a foreign tone in E minor that makes the minor third muddy. Seconds: roughness instead of tone. Sixths: foreign tones, but quiet and high enough to count as colour.

## B.5 Over E2 (82.4 Hz)

all difference tones halve: fifth → 41 Hz (E1, pressure), minor third → 15.6 Hz (below hearing, modulation only), second order 66.8 Hz ≈ C2. Hence avoid low thirds and keep fifths low.

## B.6 Rules

1. Below E3 only root, octave, fifth. 2. Thirds from E3 at medium gain, from E4 at high gain. 3. The major third tolerates more gain than the minor. 4. Under gain sixths are the better thirds (inversion upward). 5. Less gain or a low-pass before the distortion reduces intermodulation more than any EQ after it. 6. Two guitars in thirds: both with less gain than the riff, both above E3.

cC.title: Delay arithmetic and time values
cC.text:
This appendix holds the calculations for chapters 15, 16 and 23: note values in milliseconds, delay times, numbers of repeats, swing percentages, room sizes and micro timing.

## C.1 Basic formula

Quarter in ms = 60000 / BPM (BPM in quarters). Eighth = quarter / 2. Sixteenth = quarter / 4. Dotted eighth = quarter · 0.75. Eighth triplet = quarter / 3. Quarter triplet = quarter · 2/3. Half = quarter · 2. Whole = quarter · 4. In 12/8 with tempo ♩. = BPM: dotted quarter = 60000 / BPM, eighth = one third of it.

## C.2 Table (quarter · eighth · dotted eighth · eighth triplet · half), ms:



- 50: 1200 · 600 · 900 · 400 · 2400
- 55: 1091 · 545 · 818 · 364 · 2182
- 60: 1000 · 500 · 750 · 333 · 2000
- 65: 923 · 462 · 692 · 308 · 1846
- 70: 857 · 429 · 643 · 286 · 1714
- 72: 833 · 417 · 625 · 278 · 1667
- 75: 800 · 400 · 600 · 267 · 1600
- 80: 750 · 375 · 563 · 250 · 1500
- 85: 706 · 353 · 529 · 235 · 1412
- 90: 667 · 333 · 500 · 222 · 1333
- 95: 632 · 316 · 474 · 211 · 1263
- 100: 600 · 300 · 450 · 200 · 1200
- 120: 500 · 250 · 375 · 167 · 1000
- 140: 429 · 214 · 321 · 143 · 857

## C.3 Rhythmic delays

Dotted eighth over eighth notes yields a sixteenth grid (each repeat lands a sixteenth before the next attack). Quarter delay over half notes doubles the attacks. Eighth-triplet delay over straight eighths creates a shuffle feel. Two delays (quarter and dotted eighth) together give the dense U2 pattern. At doom tempi delays are long: a quarter at 60 = one second; that is already spatial.

## C.4 Feedback and number of repeats

Number of audible repeats ≈ log(0.01) / log(feedback), for a −40 dB audibility limit: feedback 30 % → 4, 50 % → 7, 70 % → 13, 90 % → 44. In practice (with filtering) about half.

## C.5 Swing percentage

Share of the first eighth in the quarter: 50 % straight, 58 % light, 62 % medium, 67 % triplet (2:1), 75 % dotted (3:1). For sixteenth swing the same at eighth level. Drum machines give swing either as a percentage, usually between 50 and 80, or as a shift of the offbeats in grid steps; in the second case the shift is converted into the percentage: shift divided by the length of a beat, plus 50.

## C.6 Pre-delay and room

Sound 343 m/s → 1 ms ≈ 34 cm. Pre-delay 10 ms ≈ first reflection after a 3.4 m detour (small room), 30 ms ≈ 10 m (hall), 60 ms ≈ 20 m (church). Reverb time RT60: time to −60 dB. Living room 0.4 s, studio 0.3 s, hall 1.5–2.5 s, church 3–8 s.

## C.7 Haas effect

Two signals less than 30–40 ms apart are heard as one, localised toward the earlier. A doubling delay of 15–25 ms without feedback widens without sounding like an echo.

## C.8 Microtiming

At ♩ = 60 a sixteenth lasts 250 ms; laid-back sits at 10–40 ms, i.e. 4–16 % of a sixteenth. Drum machines offer the shift as nudge or micro timing per hit, in milliseconds or in fractions of the grid; a grid of 1/384 bar corresponds at ♩ = 60 to a step of 10.4 ms, 1/96 bar to a step of 41.7 ms. Devices without nudge reach the same only through recording with quantisation switched off.

cE.title: Chord symbol reference
cE.text:
This appendix lists all chord symbols from chapter 10 with their tones over the three centres E, A and D, plus the degree chords of the three keys.

## D.1 Reading order

Root · type (nothing = major, m, dim/°, aug/+) · seventh (7 minor, maj7/Δ major) · extension (9, 11, 13) · alteration (b5, #5, b9, #9, #11, b13) · addition (add) · omission (no3, no5) · bass (/X). The symbol fixes tones, not spacing, doubling or duration.

## D.2 Table: symbol · over E · over A · over D



- 5 (power chord) · E B · A E · D A
- major · E G# B · A C# E · D F# A
- m · E G B · A C E · D F A
- dim / ° · E G Bb · A C Eb · D F Ab
- aug / + · E G# B# · A C# E# · D F# A#
- sus2 · E F# B · A B E · D E A
- sus4 · E A B · A D E · D G A
- 6 · E G# B C# · A C# E F# · D F# A B
- m6 · E G B C# · A C E F# · D F A B
- 7 · E G# B D · A C# E G · D F# A C

- 11 (third usually omitted) · E B D F# A · A E G B D · D A C E G

- 13 · E G# B D F# C# · A C# E G B F# · D F# A C E B

- 7#9 · E G# B D G (F##) · A C# E G C (B#) · D F# A C F (E#)
- 7#11 · E G# B D A# · A C# E G D# · D F# A C G#
- 7b5 · E G# Bb D · A C# Eb G · D F# Ab C
- maj7#11 · E G# B D# A# · A C# E G# D# · D F# A C# G#
- m6/9 · E G B C# F# · A C E F# B · D F A B E

## D.3 Slash chords

X/Y: chord X with bass tone Y. Em/G first inversion, Em/B second. Em/C is not an Em chord over C but sounds as Cmaj7 without a doubled root; if C is the bass, the chord is called Cmaj7. Rule: if the bass tone is a chord tone, it is an inversion; if not, it is usually a different chord with a different name. Em/D is Em7 in third inversion. D/E is an Esus sound (E D F# A), often written E9sus4.

## D.4 Degrees in E Aeolian (triads · seventh chords)

i Em · Em7; ii° F#dim · F#m7b5; III G · Gmaj7; iv Am · Am7; v Bm · Bm7; VI C · Cmaj7; VII D · D7. Harmonic minor changes: V B · B7; vii° D#dim · D#dim7; III+ G+ · Gmaj7#5. Melodic minor additionally changes: ii F#m · F#m7; IV A · A7; vi° C#dim · C#m7b5.

## D.5 Degrees in A Aeolian

Am, Bdim, C, Dm, Em, F, G; harmonic: E, G#dim. **In D Aeolian.** Dm, Edim, F, Gm, Am, Bb, C; harmonic: A, C#dim.

## D.6 Common symbols in this book

Power chords with 5 for the distorted guitar (chapter 9). Plain triads Em, C, D, Am, G, B for modal harmony (chapter 11). madd9 and maj7 as pads without direction (chapter 10). Dominant sevenths, dim7 and the Picardy third at cadences (chapters 11 and 13). sus4 → 3 as suspension (chapter 18).

## D.7 Notation of one's own pieces

Symbols above the notes are commentary; the notes are binding. For power chords write the symbol with 5, not the triad name, so that the missing third is documented.
